text_kjv: And it came to pass, after the year was expired, at the time when kings go forth to battle, that David sent Joab, and his servants with him, and all Israel; and they destroyed the children of Ammon, and besieged Rabbah. But David tarried still at Jerusalem.

commentary.narrative:
This verse establishes the tragic irony that will structure the entire chapter: the correct moment for war has arrived, kings are doing what kings do—marching out—yet David sends others and remains behind. The phrase "after the year was expired, at the time when kings go forth to battle" marks spring, when winter rains have ended and campaigns become feasible. This is not a moment for a king to be idle. The Covenant Rendering's emphasis on le-et tset ha-melakhim ('at the time of the going-out of kings') uses an active participle construction that conveys the habitual, almost inevitable nature of the practice: this is what kings do. David's failure to go is a departure from his identity as warrior-king.

The contrast between David's sending and his remaining is the narrative hinge of the entire chapter. The TCR notes rightly identify this as "the weight of absence." The verb yoshev ('was staying' or 'tarried') in a military context is not neutral—it is a shirking, a failure of martial duty. David is home while his army fights. The text does not yet explain why, but the proximity to his bed (v. 2) and the evening rest that follows suggest a king at leisure when he should be at war. This violation of the warrior-king's covenant responsibility opens the space into which temptation enters.

The verb shalach ('sent') appears here for the first time in what will become the dominant verb of the chapter, functioning as a structural and theological marker. As the TCR notes, David will send eight times in this chapter—sending the army, sending to inquire about the woman, sending messengers to bring her, sending word to Joab, sending word about Uriah, sending Uriah back, and sending a death warrant. This verb transforms David from actor into operator of distance: he acts exclusively through intermediaries, seeing nothing directly, controlling everything indirectly. The machinery of power will become the machinery of concealment.

word_study.meaning: to send, to dispatch, to let loose, to stretch out. The root carries the sense of extending power at a distance—through an agent or messenger rather than direct action.
word_study.significance: This verb is the defining grammar of 2 Samuel 11. It appears at least eight times in the chapter, structuring the narrative as a portrait of a king who acts exclusively through delegation and distance. The TCR identifies it as the 'dominant verb of 2 Samuel 11,' and its escalation marks David's descent: sending an army (legitimate), sending an inquiry (questionable), sending messengers (predatory), sending a death warrant (murderous). The verb also echoes the warning of 1 Samuel 8:11-17, where shalach appears repeatedly in the anti-monarchy speech to describe what a king will 'take'—what a king will appropriate by power. Here, David is enacting the very predation Samuel warned Israel about.

word_study.meaning: to sit, to dwell, to remain, to abide. In a military context, the verb can mean simply to remain in place or to be idle.
word_study.significance: The TCR notes that in this military context, yashav carries 'the weight of absence.' David is sitting when he should be marching. The verb will recur at v. 2 in the phrase 'he sat in the tent door,' suggesting a pattern of leisure and inactivity. For a warrior-king, yashav is a posture of abdication.

word_study.term_english: turn of the year / when the year was expired
word_study.meaning: At the turning/returning of the year; the cyclical renewal of the calendar year. This phrase marks the spring campaign season.
word_study.significance: The TCR explains that this phrase marks 'the season when kings march out to war.' The root teshuvah carries the sense of return or turning—the year has cycled, and military campaigns resume as predictably as seasons. This is the rhythm of ancient Near Eastern warfare: winter was dormant, spring meant movement. David's refusal to move with this rhythm is an abdication of military and kingly duty.

word_study.meaning: to corrupt, to spoil, to ruin, to destroy, to lay waste. Can mean physical destruction or moral corruption.
word_study.significance: The verb shachat will echo through the narrative in more than one sense. Here it describes the legitimate destruction of the Ammonites—the proper work of war. But the chapter itself will become a story of corruption and moral destruction. The narrator uses the same verbal root to describe military success (v. 1) and the corruption of David's character through the actions that follow.

cross_references.connection: Samuel's warning about what a king will do: he will 'take' sons, daughters, fields, and wealth by force. David is now enacting precisely this predatory model of kingship through the verb shalach (sending agents to appropriate what belongs to others).

Uriah the Hittite appears in the list of David's thirty mighty men. The reader learns that David knows Uriah personally and has benefited from his loyalty and valor in battle. This makes David's later action a betrayal of a soldier whose life he depends upon.

The law for a future king prohibits him from multiplying horses (instruments of war) or wives (sources of temptation). David's failure to go to war and his subsequent seduction both violate these warnings about royal restraint.

Earlier narrative of David's military prowess and his identity as a warrior-king. The contrast between David's active, martial presence in earlier chapters and his passive idleness here marks a spiritual and ethical decline.
Later reference to Joab's role in the Ammonite war. The text suggests Joab knew more than he said, and David's manipulation of his commander will have consequences for the entire kingdom.

commentary.historical_context: The phrase 'at the time when kings go forth to battle' reflects the actual military rhythm of the ancient Near East. Campaigns began in spring (March-April) when the winter rains had ended and the earth dried enough to support marching armies and siege equipment. Archaeological evidence from the Ammonite period shows Rabbah was a fortified city that would require sustained siege. The reference to Uriah as 'the Hittite' is notable—the Hittite kingdom had fallen by David's time (c. 1000 BCE), so Uriah is likely a foreign mercenary or the descendant of one, which made him even more dependent on David's favor and protection. Ancient Near Eastern royal practice included sending subordinate commanders on campaign while the king remained in the capital for administrative and religious duties, but this was not universal practice, and certainly not standard for the warrior-kings of early Israel. David's remaining in Jerusalem is presented as a departure from what is expected and appropriate.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: The pattern of a leader's fall through unauthorized use of power mirrors warnings in the Book of Mormon about kings and judges who abuse authority. Alma 51:35-36 describes how Amalickiah gained power through 'cunning devices and flattery,' using others as tools for his ambitions—much like David's use of shalach here. The contrast between righteous and unrighteous use of delegated authority recurs throughout the Book of Mormon.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 121:36-37 directly addresses the misuse of priesthood power: 'That the rights of the priesthood are inseparably connected with the powers of heaven, and that the powers of heaven cannot be controlled nor handled only upon the principles of righteousness. That they may be conferred upon us, it is true; but when we undertake to cover our sins, or to gratify our pride, our vain ambition, or to exercise control or dominion or compulsion upon the souls of the children of men, in any degree of unrighteousness, behold, the heavens withdraw themselves.' David's use of shalach to accomplish a transgression is exactly the kind of 'covering sins' and 'exercising dominion' that separates one from divine approval.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: David's failure to fulfill his covenant duty as a warrior-king parallels the temple principle of complete consecration. A covenant made before God requires full obedience and personal presence, not delegation of responsibility. David's abdication of his martial duty is a first step toward the fuller abdication that follows—the avoidance of Uriah's presence, the denial of accountability, the manipulation of law and witness.

commentary.christological_typology: While David serves as a type of Christ in many contexts (shepherd king, covenant restorer, messianic forerunner), this chapter deliberately undermines that typology. Here David becomes anti-type—a king who fails his covenantal duty, acts through corrupt intermediaries, and uses his power to prey on the vulnerable. The contrast highlights the nature of Christ's kingship: Jesus acts with personal presence and moral accountability, suffers personally for his people rather than sending others to suffer, and uses his power to serve rather than to appropriate.
commentary.application: For modern covenant members, this verse introduces the danger of spiritual idleness at critical moments. When we are called to act—to bear testimony, to serve in our assignments, to stand against injustice—the excuse to send others or to remain passive can open the door to temptation and transgression. The principle that appears here is that distance from direct responsibility creates distance from moral awareness. David cannot see the consequences of his actions when he delegates everything through shalach. Conversely, personal presence and direct accountability in our covenant duties keep us morally alert. The verse also warns against the assumption that power—rightly held in most circumstances—can be used wrongly without consequence. A king may legitimately send armies, but the same mechanism of power becomes corrupting when directed toward private desires.

text_kjv: And it came to pass in an eveningtide, that David arose from off his bed, and walked upon the roof of the king's house: and from the roof he saw a woman washing herself; and the woman was very beautiful to look upon.

commentary.narrative:
The temporal marker le-et ha-erev ('toward the time of evening') places this moment in the golden hour when the heat breaks and rooftops become living spaces in ancient Near Eastern domestic life. But for David, this should be the time of military council, not personal leisure. He rises from his mishkavo (bed, couch)—indicating an afternoon rest that a king actively campaigning would not take. The TCR notes directly: 'A king at war would not be napping; a king at home has nothing else to do.' This detail establishes David's idleness not as a moment of repose in a busy day, but as the underlying condition of a king who has delegated his responsibilities entirely.

The verb va-yar ('he saw') is presented without context—no indication that David sought anything, no suggestion of intention. The narrator maintains strict objectivity: David simply saw. Yet everything that will follow flows from this moment of seeing and the decision to act on what was seen. This is not presented as entrapment or as the inevitable weakness of the flesh, but as a choice—a moment where David could have turned away but did not. The TCR translates it plainly: 'From the roof he saw a woman bathing.'

The description of Bathsheba as tovat mar'eh me'od ('very good of appearance') carries specific biblical weight. The TCR notes that this same construction is used for Sarah, Rebekah, and Rachel—women whose beauty sets narratives in motion and whose physical appearance carries covenantal significance. But the narrator offers no context, no romantic language, no justification: just the bare statement that she was beautiful. This is the narrator's only characterization of Bathsheba in this chapter. She exists in the text primarily as the object of male action and male gaze.

word_study.meaning: he rose up, he stood up, he awakened. The verb can indicate simple physical rising or can carry a sense of purposeful action.
word_study.significance: In context, va-yaqom indicates David rising from his bed at evening time. The verb is neutral in itself, but paired with his afternoon napping (while his army fights) and his rooftop walk, it suggests a man with leisure time and no urgent business—the opposite of what a warrior-king should be doing.

word_study.meaning: he walked, he went about, he strolled. Can indicate casual movement or purposeful journey.
word_study.significance: The verb va-yithallekh, meaning 'he walked,' suggests David's movement on the roof is a leisurely stroll, not a purposeful errand. He is in a position (on the roof of the royal palace) where he can see into the privacy of his neighbor's home. The casual nature of the verb contrasts sharply with the consequences of what he sees.

word_study.meaning: he saw, he beheld, he perceived. One of the most fundamental verbs in Hebrew narrative.
word_study.significance: The narrator uses the simplest possible verb for this moment—va-yar, 'he saw.' No indication of intent to look, no search or seeking: David simply saw. Yet this seeing will trigger a cascade of increasingly serious transgressions. The verb is theologically significant in the Hebrew Bible; seeing can be the beginning of covenantal awareness (as in theophany narratives) or, as here, the beginning of transgression. Genesis 3:6 uses the same verb when Eve 'saw' the forbidden fruit.

word_study.meaning: washing, bathing, cleansing. The participle form rochetzet suggests an ongoing action.
word_study.significance: The verb rochetzet, 'bathing' or 'washing herself,' appears in the masculine plural form in the Hebrew (me-al ha-gag), indicating she is washing on her roof—a private domestic action. Her bathing is presented as a normal, lawful, private act. She is not displayed; she is caught in a moment of private self-care. The fact that she is bathing on the roof (visible from the king's roof) suggests either the physical layout of Jerusalem's rooftops or the vulnerability of private space to royal gaze.

word_study.meaning: good of appearance, beautiful to look upon. A construct phrase indicating beauty as a visual quality.
word_study.significance: The specific phrase tovat mar'eh me'od ('very beautiful to look upon') is used in Genesis for the patriarchal wives (Sarah, Rebekah, Rachel). The narrator places Bathsheba in this covenantal genealogy through this single description. Yet the use is paradoxical: the same language that describes women central to the covenant promise is applied to a woman who will become the object of covenant violation. Her beauty is a fact, not a justification for what David will do.

cross_references.connection: Eve 'saw' (va-tar) the tree was good for food and pleasing to the eye, and she took. David 'sees' (va-yar) the woman is beautiful, and he will take. Both narratives begin with seeing and proceed to transgression.

Abraham mentions that Sarah is beautiful (tovat mar'eh), and pharaoh 'sees' her and takes her into his house. The pattern of seeing and taking appears in multiple covenant contexts with tragic results.

'Lust not after her beauty in thine heart... For by means of a whorish woman a man is brought to a piece of bread.' The wisdom tradition explicitly warns against allowing the sight of beauty to lead to transgression.
Job declares: 'I made a covenant with mine eyes; why then should I think upon a maid?' Job's covenant discipline stands in stark contrast to David's lack of restraint.
Jesus teaches that to 'look on a woman to lust after her' is to commit adultery in the heart. The seeing in this verse is not merely optical; it is the beginning of a transgression of the law.

commentary.historical_context: The layout of Jerusalem's rooftops in the 10th century BCE would have made it possible for someone on the royal palace roof to see into the courtyards and private spaces of nearby houses. Rooftops served as outdoor living spaces in ancient Near Eastern domestic architecture—places for sleeping in summer heat, for drying clothes and food, for evening leisure. The fact that Bathsheba is bathing on her roof is not unusual; what is unusual is that the king's roof overlooks her space. This suggests either the topography of Jerusalem's construction or the particular positioning of the royal palace. Archaeological evidence from Iron Age Palestinian sites shows houses with flat roofs and courtyards, confirming that such viewing could occur.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: The Book of Mormon repeatedly warns about the danger of idle leaders. Helaman 6:39 describes how secret combinations grow when leaders become 'slothful, and suffer their people to be oppressed and to be afflicted.' The Nephite cycle shows that when rulers neglect their duties and become comfortable, the opportunity for transgression increases. Mosiah 29:26-27 explains how judges fall into unrighteousness: they 'do not do the judge according to the oath.' David's idleness is the condition in which unrighteousness grows.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 88:124 teaches the importance of being actively engaged in righteous labor and duty. The principle underlying David's failure is that spiritual and moral safety come through faithful work, not through idleness. D&C 58:27 states: 'Wherefore, be faithful; and let all things be done in order.' David has abandoned order—he should be at war, not napping on his roof.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The temple principle of watchfulness is violated here. In Doctrine and Covenants 64:34, members are counseled: 'Beware of pride, lest ye become as the Nephites of old.' The root of David's transgression is the unguarded moment—the failure to maintain spiritual and moral vigilance. Modern temple covenants include the commitment to use power righteously; idle power becomes corrupted power.

commentary.christological_typology: This verse contrasts David's weakness with Christ's perfect moral governance. Christ, though he possessed full power and authority, never used his vantage point of power to appropriate or to satisfy private desire. His refusal to call down legions of angels, his refusal to turn stones to bread, his refusal to take the kingdoms offered him in the wilderness—all represent the moral restraint David lacks. Where David sees beauty and takes, Christ sees human need and serves.
commentary.application: This verse teaches the principle that unguarded moments and idle time create vulnerability to transgression. Modern covenant members are not to imagine themselves immune to temptation; the narrative presents David—a man chosen by God, anointed as king, filled with the Spirit—falling into sin. What protects us is not our inherent goodness but our faithful engagement in our covenantal duties and our willingness to maintain spiritual vigilance. The specific danger of the 'seeing' moment is that it precedes choice: we cannot always control what we see, but we can control what we do with what we see. Job's covenant with his eyes (Job 31:1) and Jesus's teaching about lust in the heart (Matthew 5:28) both point to the principle that moral life begins in the moment of sight—in what we choose to do with what we see.

text_kjv: And David sent and enquired after the woman. And one said, Is not this Bathsheba, the daughter of Eliam, the wife of Uriah the Hittite?

commentary.narrative:
The verb shalach appears for the second time in the chapter, and now it is paired with darash ('to inquire, to seek out, to investigate'). David's response to seeing the woman is not to turn away but to make a deliberate, active investigation. The TCR notes that this 'is not casual curiosity but active intelligence-gathering.' David sends someone to gather information about the woman's identity. The text presents no hesitation, no moment of conscience, only the swift machinery of royal inquiry.

The response comes back as a triple identification, each element designed to stop David but each element he will set aside. Bathsheba is presented as: (1) daughter of Sheba/oath (bat-Sheva), (2) daughter of Eliam, and (3) wife of Uriah the Hittite. The third identification is the critical one. Uriah appears in 2 Samuel 23:39 as one of David's thirty mighty men—the elite warriors on whom the kingdom's defense depends. The narrator ensures the reader understands: David knows Uriah. David has benefited from his valor. Uriah is fighting in David's war right now, risking his life for the king who is about to betray him.

The phrasing 'Is not this Bathsheba' (haloa zot Bat-Sheva) is framed as a question, as though the inquirer is confirming what David may already know. This leaves open the possibility that David already knew Uriah's wife by sight or reputation. The TCR notes that Eliam may be the son of Ahithophel, making Bathsheba of high family—not a vulnerable peasant but a woman of rank and family connection. All of this makes David's action an act of taking not from the powerless but from a man of standing whose loyalty David has relied upon.

word_study.meaning: Shalach: to send, to dispatch. Darash: to seek, to investigate, to inquire, to search out with intention.
word_study.significance: The pairing of shalach and darash reveals David's active agency. He does not passively receive information; he actively seeks it. Darash implies deliberate investigation, not casual wondering. The verb darash appears in the Bible for seeking God (Deuteronomy 4:29), for consulting prophets, for legal inquiry (Judges 5:10). Here it is used to investigate the identity of a woman David desires, transforming a private desire into an act of royal investigation. The verb indicates intention and purpose.

word_study.meaning: wife of, woman of. The construct form indicating a woman's legal marital status.
word_study.significance: The final identification—eshet Uriyah ha-Chitti ('wife of Uriah the Hittite')—is the one that should stop David. The narrator presents Bathsheba's primary identity here as a wife—a woman bound by covenant to another man. Yet this identification, which should be prohibitive, becomes merely informational. The response identifies exactly what David cannot take, and David takes it anyway.

word_study.meaning: Uriah (meaning 'God is my light' or 'my light is God') the Hittite. An ethnic designation for a man from the Hittite region or of Hittite descent.
word_study.significance: The phrase 'Uriah the Hittite' becomes a constant refrain throughout the chapter—v. 3, v. 6, v. 8, v. 11, v. 12, v. 15, v. 17, v. 21, v. 24. The repetition of his ethnic designation and his name creates a kind of accusatory litany: Uriah, Uriah, Uriah—the man whose wife you have taken, the man whose blood you will shed. The Hittite designation is noteworthy because the Hittite empire had fallen by David's time (c. 1000 BCE); Uriah is likely a foreign mercenary or the descendant of one, making him even more dependent on David's favor and protection.

cross_references.connection: Uriah the Hittite is listed among David's thirty mighty men, confirming that David knows him personally and has benefited from his military valor. The list underscores Uriah's rank and loyalty.

The seventh commandment: 'Thou shalt not commit adultery.' The identification of Bathsheba as a wife invokes the law that David is about to violate. The narrator ensures the reader knows the law being broken.
The covenant law against adultery, restated in the covenant renewal. David knows the law. The narrator presents him with full knowledge of what he is transgressing.

Samuel's warning about what a king will 'take': he will take your sons for his army, your daughters for his servants, your fields, your vineyards. David is taking Uriah's wife—enacting the very predatory behavior Samuel warned Israel a king would do.

Later, the narrator notes that David 'did that which was right in the eyes of the LORD, and turned not aside from any thing that he commanded him all the days of his life, save only in the matter of Uriah the Hittite.' This verse becomes the definitive exception that proves the rule.

commentary.historical_context: The mention that Eliam may be the son of Ahithophel (see the TCR notes and 2 Samuel 23:34) is significant because Ahithophel becomes a central figure in Absalom's rebellion (2 Samuel 15:12). Some scholars propose that Bathsheba's family connection to Ahithophel may explain why the wisest counselor in David's court turns against him: the violation of Bathsheba could have motivated Ahithophel's later defection. Whether or not this historical reconstruction is correct, the text indicates Bathsheba was of significant family rank, not a powerless woman but a woman with connections. Uriah's status as 'the Hittite' may indicate he was a foreign mercenary or professional soldier integrated into David's military structure—a common practice in ancient Near Eastern armies, where foreign soldiers of proven skill were highly valued.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: The pattern of a leader using power to investigate and then to appropriate recurs in the Book of Mormon. Alma 1:2-8 describes how Nehor uses his influence to rise in authority and then uses that authority to satisfy his vain desires. The mechanism is similar: investigation of standing, inquiry about status, then use of power to take. Mormon 8:32 warns: 'Yea, it shall come in a day when the power of God shall be denied.'
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 121:39 states: 'We have learned by sad experience that it is the nature and disposition of almost all men, as soon as they get a little authority, as they suppose, they will immediately begin to exercise unrighteous dominion.' David's inquiry reveals exactly this pattern: authority leads to investigation, investigation leads to the exercise of power without moral restraint.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The covenant to use power righteously, made in the temple, is violated here at its beginning. David has received power from God; the covenant of kingship carried expectations of restraint and righteousness. His turning that power toward the investigation and taking of Uriah's wife is a direct violation of the covenant principle that power must be exercised in righteousness.

commentary.christological_typology: Again, this verse emphasizes the contrast between David's use of power and Christ's. Christ also had access to full information—he knew all things—yet he never used that knowledge to appropriate power or to take what belonged to another. His knowledge was always directed toward healing, teaching, and redemption, never toward possession or control.
commentary.application: This verse teaches that the moment of investigation is critical. What information do we seek? What do we do with knowledge? For David, the inquiry itself is a form of transgression—it is the decision to gather information in service of an unlawful desire. Modern covenant members should recognize that the seeking of information 'that we should not know' or the investigation of how to accomplish something forbidden is itself a form of turning from righteousness. The verse also teaches that we cannot claim ignorance as a defense. David is informed that Bathsheba is another man's wife. He has full knowledge of the law and the status of the woman. He chooses to proceed anyway. The principle is that knowledge of the law makes transgression more serious, not less.

text_kjv: And David sent messengers, and took her; and she came in unto him, and he lay with her; for she was purified from her uncleanness: and she returned unto her house.

commentary.narrative:
This verse contains three instances of shalach (David 'sent') and introduces the verb laqach ('took'), establishing the grammar of royal seizure. The TCR notes that the pairing of shalach and laqach—'sent and took'—is the language of royal appropriation, the very warning Samuel gave Israel in 1 Samuel 8:11-17. The verb laqach appears seven times in that anti-monarchy speech to describe what a king will appropriate by force. David is enacting precisely what Samuel warned Israel a king would do.

But notice the remarkable compression of action: no dialogue, no courtship, no resistance, no consent, no indication of Bathsheba's response or agency. The narrator uses a series of verbs of action, but only some of them have David as subject. Bathsheba comes (va-tavo), she is with him (immah), he lies with her (va-yishkav immah), she returns (va-tashav)—all presented in the simple past tense, all compressed into the bare minimum of narrative. The text gives the reader no access to Bathsheba's inner state or to any dialogue between them. She is grammatically passive throughout: she is taken, she comes, she is lain with, she returns. The effect is to present her as the object of royal action, not as an agent in her own story.

The parenthetical about her purification—'she had just purified herself from her monthly period'—is clinical in its precision. The Hebrew mitqaddeshet mi-tum'atah indicates she had completed her menstrual cycle and was ritually pure. The narrator inserts this detail to close off any possible escape: no one can claim the child is another man's. The detail is presented with the same detached precision that characterizes the entire chapter. The narrator is not justifying David or Bathsheba; the narrator is presenting facts with surgical coldness.

word_study.meaning: to take, to seize, to grasp, to appropriate, to bring. Can indicate taking by force or taking in marriage, depending on context.
word_study.significance: The verb laqach is the defining verb of this verse and carries immense theological weight in the Hebrew Bible. It appears seven times in 1 Samuel 8:11-17 in Samuel's anti-monarchy warning: the king will take your sons, your daughters, your fields, your vineyards, your servants. Laqach paired with shalach creates the grammar of royal predation. In context—'David sent messengers and took her'—the verb indicates appropriation without consent, seizure of what belongs to another. It is the opposite of the consensual taking of marriage; it is the taking of property.

word_study.meaning: to send, to dispatch, to extend power at a distance.
word_study.significance: Third occurrence of shalach in the narrative. David now sends messengers (mal'akhim—the same word used for angels or divine messengers, here deployed for an act of predation). The escalation is unmistakable: sent the army (v. 1), sent an inquiry (v. 3), sent for the woman (v. 4). The verb structures the entire chapter as a cascade of delegated transgressions.

word_study.meaning: came to him, came unto him. The verb bo'ah indicates movement from one place to another.
word_study.significance: The phrase va-tavo elayv ('she came unto him') presents Bathsheba's only apparent agency in the verse—she comes to him. Yet this 'coming' is the result of being summoned by the king's messengers. She has no choice whether to come; a woman summoned by the king could not refuse. The narrator's use of the verb of coming, rather than 'was brought,' maintains the surface appearance of her agency while the context (she was taken) reveals its absence.

word_study.meaning: to lie, to recline, to lie down with, to have sexual relations. In the context of marriage or covenant relationships, the verb can be neutral; in the context of violation, it indicates sexual act without consent.
word_study.significance: The verb va-yishkav immah ('he lay with her') is used throughout the Hebrew Bible for sexual relations in various contexts. Here, paired with the taking and the absence of consent or dialogue, it describes a sexual act that occurs without Bathsheba's agency or voice.

word_study.meaning: purifying herself from her impurity/uncleanness. The participial construction mitqaddeshet (fem. sing.) indicates an action in progress or just completed. Tum'ah (impurity/uncleanness) refers to menstrual impurity.
word_study.significance: The clause is a parenthetical temporal marker establishing that Bathsheba has completed her menstrual cycle and is ritually pure (see Leviticus 15:19-28). The detail is medically/biologically significant: she has not been with any man recently, so any pregnancy can only be David's. The narrator inserts this clinical fact to eliminate any possible ambiguity about paternity and to underscore the inevitability of the pregnancy that will follow. The use of the participial form mitqaddeshet is ambiguous—it could mean 'she was purifying herself' or 'she had purified herself'—but the context (she is now ready to be with David) suggests the action is completed or nearly completed.

cross_references.connection: Samuel warns that a king will 'take' (laqach) your sons, daughters, fields, and servants. David's taking of Bathsheba through shalach (sending) and laqach (taking) enacts the predatory kingship Samuel warned against.
Laws of menstrual impurity and purification. The detail that Bathsheba was purified establishes her ritual status and the biological certainty of paternity.

The commandment against adultery is invoked implicitly by the narrator's compressed account of the act. No justification, no emotional language, only the bare act of taking and lying with another man's wife.

Paul teaches that sexual sin is unique in that it violates the body in a way other sins do not. The narrator's cold presentation of the act emphasizes the violation—no romance, no consent, no mitigating emotion.

commentary.historical_context: The menstrual purification laws in Leviticus 15:19-28 were practiced in ancient Israel and were understood as a form of ritual impurity that rendered a woman temporarily ineligible for sexual relations. Bathsheba's purification, therefore, marks her as eligible for marital relations—either legitimately with her husband Uriah or (in David's case) as the target of his appropriation. The TCR's note that she 'had just purified herself' suggests the timing is significant: she is at the point of ritual eligibility, making any resulting pregnancy unmistakably attributable to David. In ancient Near Eastern culture, a king's sexual acquisition of another man's wife was not uncommon, though it remained a violation of covenant law.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: The pattern of a leader using delegated authority to accomplish transgression while maintaining distance from direct responsibility appears throughout the Book of Mormon. Alma 51 describes Amalickiah using 'cunning devices' and agents to accomplish his aims. The principle that delegated authority becomes corrupted when used for unrighteous purposes is central to the Book of Mormon's political teaching.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 121:39-46 directly addresses the abuse of priesthood power. David's use of shalach to take Bathsheba—using the machinery of kingship to accomplish a private transgression—parallels the unrighteous dominion warned against in section 121. The passage teaches that 'the heavens withdraw themselves' when power is used to 'cover our sins' or to 'gratify our pride, our vain ambition.'
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The temple covenant includes the promise to use power, position, and influence righteously and for the benefit of others, not for private appropriation. David's taking of Bathsheba through delegated authority violates the most basic principle of the covenant—that power is a sacred trust, not a personal prerogative. The principle of 'no compulsion' in D&C 58:26-28 directly condemns what David does here: his use of the machinery of kingship to compel Bathsheba's presence.

commentary.christological_typology: This verse presents the anti-type to Christ's character most starkly. Christ, possessing absolute power, never took anything by force or compulsion. His refusal to 'take' the kingdoms offered him in the wilderness (Matthew 4:8-10), his refusal to grasp at divine prerogative (Philippians 2:5-8), his consistent yielding of personal will to the Father's will—all stand in absolute contrast to David's seizure of another's wife.
commentary.application: This verse teaches several principles for modern covenant members. First, distance from direct responsibility does not remove moral responsibility. David sent messengers rather than coming himself, but he remains fully culpable. We cannot delegate away moral accountability. Second, the use of power and position to accomplish private desires, especially desires that violate covenant law, is transgression. The grammar of David's action—sending, taking, lying with—should be recognized in modern contexts whenever power is used to appropriate, compel, or violate. Third, the narrator's silence about Bathsheba's response should disturb us. When the narrator refuses to give voice to someone in a situation of unequal power, we should hear that as a sign of violation. Healthy covenant relationships include consent, voice, and agency.

text_kjv: And the woman conceived, and sent and told David, and said, I am with child.

commentary.narrative:
Two Hebrew words detonate the chapter's catastrophe: harah anokhi ('pregnant I am'). This is Bathsheba's first and only speech in 2 Samuel 11, and it is the shortest possible statement of biological fact. No plea, no accusation, no request for help—just the statement that will unravel everything David has done and everything he will yet do. The TCR notes the extraordinary economy of her speech: 'Two words. No elaboration, no emotion, no appeal.' 

More significant still is the shift in narrative agency. For the first time in the chapter, someone other than David sends. Va-tishlach—she sent. The verb shalach, which has belonged exclusively to David in verses 1, 3, and 4, is now used by Bathsheba. Yet what she sends is not a messenger or a command but a fact—a biological reality that David cannot control, cannot retract, and cannot hide. Where David's sendings have been acts of power and appropriation, Bathsheba's sending is an act of communication about a consequence beyond both their control.

The pregnancy is the hinge point of the narrative. In verse 4, David lies with Bathsheba, and the text records no immediate consequence. But pregnancy follows inevitably, and with it comes the crisis that will drive all of David's subsequent actions. The TCR notes that 'a pregnancy cannot be unsent.' What was conceived in secrecy and sin now has a voice—Bathsheba's voice—announcing it to the man who caused it. This moment marks the transition from transgression to cover-up, from sin to murder.

word_study.meaning: to be pregnant, to conceive, to become with child. The verb is often simple and declarative in biblical narrative.
word_study.significance: The verb harah is used straightforwardly to announce pregnancy throughout scripture (Genesis 16:4, Judges 13:3, 1 Samuel 1:20). Here, it is the announcement of a fact that changes everything. The verb carries no moral judgment in itself—it is a biological reality—but in context it announces the consequence of David's transgression.

word_study.meaning: she sent, she dispatched. The feminine form of the verb shalach.
word_study.significance: This is the first occurrence of shalach with a subject other than David. The verb now belongs to Bathsheba, and what she sends is not a messenger or an order but a message—information that will set in motion David's descent into increasingly serious transgression. The shift in agency is crucial: David's sendings have been active exertions of power; Bathsheba's sending is a communication of fact. Yet the verb is the same, suggesting that even this act of communication uses the machinery of royal (or at least personal) authority to get the message through.

word_study.meaning: I am pregnant, I am with child. An emphatic personal statement using the independent pronoun anokhi ('I').
word_study.significance: The use of the independent pronoun anokhi ('I') gives weight to Bathsheba's statement: 'I [emphatic] am pregnant.' The two-word statement is Bathsheba's only speech in the chapter, and its brevity makes it all the more powerful. No elaboration, no appeal, no question—just the fact that she alone can state with absolute certainty.

cross_references.connection: Judah's statement 'She is more righteous than I' when he discovers Tamar's pregnancy. Pregnancy as a consequence that cannot be hidden and forces moral reckoning.
Hannah's prayer is answered with conception; 'and she conceived.' In contrast to Bathsheba's pregnancy, which results from violation, Hannah's conception is presented as an answer to faithful prayer.
Mary's announcement of her pregnancy is presented with consent, understanding, and covenant. The contrast to Bathsheba's silent conception in violation is striking.
The end of the chapter references the pregnancy again: 'She was with child by David.' The pregnancy structures the entire narrative.

commentary.historical_context: In ancient Israel, pregnancy outside of marriage or pregnancy as a result of violation created severe social and legal consequences for the woman. Bathsheba's announcement to David is a necessity—she cannot hide or conceal a pregnancy, and the father (David) must respond. The social reality is that Bathsheba's situation is now critical: she cannot remain married to Uriah with David's child in her womb. The only options available to her involve David's intervention—either he must appear to be the father (somehow, which will require elaborate deception) or he must somehow solve the problem. The pregnancy creates an impossible situation that will drive David toward increasingly serious transgressions.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: The idea that consequences cannot be hidden or unsent appears throughout the Book of Mormon. Alma 12:14 states: 'All things which have been revealed unto the children of men shall at that day be revealed; therefore they are made known according to the record which is kept.' The pregnancy is a fact that cannot be concealed; it announces itself.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 121:37 teaches that when one 'undertakes to cover our sins... the heavens withdraw themselves; the Spirit of the Lord is grieved.' The pregnancy is the consequence David cannot hide, and it will drive him to more serious attempts at concealment.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The covenant principle that all is known to God is invoked implicitly by the pregnancy—a fact visible to all, a consequence that cannot be hidden. The temple teaches that we cannot hide from God or from the consequences of our actions.

commentary.christological_typology: The pregnancy, in the context of this narrative, becomes a type of the consequences of sin that cannot be hidden or denied. Christ, by contrast, bore the consequences of all sin in his own person through the Atonement, transforming the possibility of cover-up into the possibility of repentance and redemption.
commentary.application: This verse teaches that consequences cannot be unsent or hidden indefinitely. What we have sown will be reaped; what has been conceived will be born; what is done in secret will be revealed. For modern covenant members, the principle is both warning and comfort: warning that transgression will have consequences we cannot control or hide, comfort that the truth will eventually emerge and enable either repentance or accountability. The verse also teaches the power of plain speech. Bathsheba's simple statement—'I am pregnant'—is more powerful than any accusation or plea could be. Sometimes the most powerful thing we can do is state the truth plainly and let it speak for itself.

text_kjv: And David sent to Joab, saying, Send me Uriah the Hittite. And Joab sent Uriah to David.

commentary.narrative:
This verse contains three instances of shalach in rapid succession: David sends (va-yishlach David), saying send (shelach elai), and Joab sent (va-yishlach Yo'av). The TCR notes that 'the triple repetition in a single verse is a deliberate literary effect—the narrator is hammering the verb into the reader's consciousness.' The entire machinery of royal bureaucracy is activated to address a personal crisis. Joab obeys without question; the text gives no indication that he knows David's motive or understands what David intends.

But Joab would know the context. Uriah is one of David's thirty mighty men, a warrior of reputation. Joab is currently commanding the siege of Rabbah. For Joab to pull a skilled warrior from an active siege requires explanation—and yet no explanation is given. The text presents Joab's obedience as immediate and unquestioning. This could indicate that Joab trusts David completely or that the king's word is absolute and requires no justification. But it also suggests that Joab might already suspect something: why would the king summon one specific soldier from the siege if not for a private purpose?

The phrase 'Uriah the Hittite' is repeated for the fifth time in the narrative (vv. 3, 6 twice, and the name alone establishes his identity). The repetition becomes a kind of accusatory litany: every mention of Uriah's name is a reminder of the man whose wife David has taken and whose blood David will soon shed. The narrative is inexorably moving toward Uriah's death, and his name becomes a constant presence in the text—a witness to what has been done and what will be done.

word_study.meaning: to send, to dispatch, to command by sending a message.
word_study.significance: The triple occurrence of shalach in a single verse (va-yishlach David, shelach elai, va-yishlach Yo'av) is a deliberate literary device. The verb appears so rapidly that the sentence reads like a machine operating at full speed: send, send, send. David's power operates entirely through delegation, and the entire machinery of the kingdom is deployed to solve his personal problem. The verb has become so frequent by this point (it appears at least five times in verses 1-6) that it has become the signature verb of the chapter—the word that structures David's entire descent into transgression and murder. Each sending escalates the gravity of what is being sent for: sending an army (legitimate), sending an inquiry (questionable), sending messengers for a woman (predatory), and now sending for a soldier (covering up transgression).

word_study.meaning: saying, to say. The infinitive form (le-emor) introduces reported speech. Elai means 'to me' or 'unto me.'
word_study.significance: The phrase 'David sent to Joab, saying' (va-yishlach David el-Yo'av le-emor) introduces David's command to his commander. The verb emor (say) is used to convey royal commands, prophecies, and divine speech in biblical narrative. Here, it is used for David's urgent request—shaped like a command—to bring Uriah.

cross_references.connection: Uriah appears in the list of David's thirty mighty men. He is a soldier of proven valor and loyalty, making his death all the more tragic and David's betrayal all the more profound.

Saul's earlier use of delegated authority: 'Saul said unto Ahijah, Bring hither the ark of God.' Like David, Saul uses authority to accomplish his purposes. The comparison suggests that the misuse of delegated power is a recurring pattern of failed kingship.
Nathan's parable presents David with a parallel situation: a man of power taking what belongs to a poor man. The parable mirrors what David has done and prepares him for accountability.

Later, David will use Joab again—sending a letter to Joab commanding him to put Uriah in the front of the battle where he will be killed. The pattern of delegating transgression through Joab continues.

commentary.historical_context: The military context is critical. Joab is commanding the siege of Rabbah, one of the most significant military campaigns of David's reign. To pull a warrior from an active siege requires justification. The fact that Joab complies without apparent hesitation could suggest either absolute obedience to the king, blind trust in David's judgment, or suspicion about David's motives. Joab's later involvement in the cover-up (vv. 14-15) suggests he eventually understands at least some of what is happening. In ancient Near Eastern military hierarchies, a king's summons was absolute; a commander could not refuse. But the text does not explain Joab's response to this request, which may be narratively significant.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: The pattern of a leader using the machinery of authority to serve personal ends, with subordinates obedient but potentially questioning, appears in the Nephite political narrative. Alma 51 describes how Amalickiah uses 'flattery' and 'cunning devices' to move the kingdom toward his purposes, with various actors complying, questioning, or seeing through his schemes.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 121:39 teaches: 'We have learned by sad experience that it is the nature and disposition of almost all men, as soon as they get a little authority, as they suppose, they will immediately begin to exercise unrighteous dominion.' David's use of his authority to summon Uriah, ostensibly for war business but actually for personal purposes, illustrates this principle exactly.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The covenant principle that authority is delegated by God and must be exercised in righteousness is violated here. David uses the authority given him for personal rather than public purposes. The temple teaches that power is a sacred trust; using it for private benefit violates the covenant.

commentary.christological_typology: This verse continues to emphasize the contrast between David's delegated and self-serving use of power and Christ's direct, self-giving exercise of authority. Christ never delegated his presence; he was personally present to those he served. He never used his authority to serve private purposes; everything he did was for others' redemption.
commentary.application: This verse teaches the principle that the use of delegated authority for personal purposes is transgression, even when those we command obey without question. The fact that Joab complies does not make David's request righteous. Authority in any form—whether kingship, leadership, priesthood, or management—carries a covenant obligation to use that power for the benefit of others and the furtherance of God's purposes, not for personal satisfaction or the solving of personal problems. The triple shalach in this verse suggests how quickly the machinery of power can be mobilized when someone in authority decides to use it for transgression. What should take time and deliberation (summoning a soldier from a siege) happens instantly. Conversely, this should prompt us to examine our own use of authority: Are we using it to serve others or to serve ourselves? Are we willing to move aside when our personal interests conflict with our responsibilities?

text_kjv: And when Uriah was come unto him, David demanded of him how Joab did, and how the people did, and how the war prospered.

commentary.narrative:
David summons Uriah from the battlefield, ostensibly to inquire about the conduct of the war. The triple repetition of 'how'—asking about Joab, the people, and the war itself—creates the illusion of a diligent commander concerned with his forces. In reality, as The Covenant Rendering notes, this is a smokescreen. David does not care about the answers; he needs Uriah in Jerusalem long enough to consummate his relationship with Bathsheba and obscure the paternity of the child she carries. The text records what David asks, not why he asks, allowing the reader to sense the grotesque disparity between the king's outward role and his hidden motive.

The language of shalom ('peace, welfare, wholeness') applied to war is almost oxymoronic. David inquires about the 'peace of the war'—a phrase that would be jarring to any Hebrew ear. This rhetorical irony deepens as the passage unfolds: David speaks of peace while plotting destruction, speaks of welfare while arranging death. Uriah, a Hittite, will soon prove to understand the covenantal meaning of the Ark and the solidarity of soldiers far better than the anointed king of Israel.

word_study.meaning: to ask, inquire, question; can also mean to request or demand. The root carries the sense of directed inquiry or solicitation.
word_study.significance: David's question is framed as a formal inquiry, the kind a commander would make to assess his forces. Yet the verb's directedness masks the manipulative purpose behind the inquiry. David asks strategically, not genuinely.

word_study.meaning: peace, wholeness, well-being, prosperity, safety. The Hebrew word encompasses not merely the absence of conflict but a state of completeness and right relationship.
word_study.significance: The triple use of shalom in a single verse—li-shlom Yo'av, li-shlom ha-am, li-shlom ha-milchamah—creates a bitter irony. David speaks the language of peace while his heart is bent on deception and ultimately murder. The word that should characterize the covenant community becomes a mask for covenant-breaking.

word_study.meaning: to send, dispatch, release; in this context, the war 'goes forward' or 'advances.' The root meaning suggests movement and agency.
word_study.significance: Though the TCR rendering uses 'welfare of the war,' the underlying sense is movement—the war's progression, its advancement. David's inquiry touches on military success even as he orchestrates personal failure.

cross_references.connection: When Abraham greets his divine visitors, he offers them rest and says, 'wash your feet'—the exact phrase David will soon use with Uriah, revealing that even gracious hospitality can be deployed as a tool of manipulation.

David's earlier inquiry about Nabal's welfare mirrors this pattern: he sends servants to inquire about someone's well-being before moving against them, suggesting that David has a habit of false courtesy preceding betrayal.

The repeated emphasis on shalom in David's false inquiry contrasts with the proverb that 'love covereth all sins'—David seeks to cover his sin with courteous words, but words without genuine shalom are empty.
The prophet condemns those who cry 'Peace, peace' when there is no peace—an echo of David's hollow inquiry about welfare in the midst of his conspiracy.
Uriah's response will reveal the difference between asking about shalom and living it: he refuses comfort out of covenantal solidarity, while David's shalom-language masks disloyalty.

commentary.historical_context: In ancient Near Eastern court protocol, a king's inquiry about his commanders and troops was both a practical necessity and a display of royal authority and concern. David's summons of Uriah follows the pattern of a concerned monarch taking counsel from a trusted soldier. However, the summoning of a battlefield officer to the capital was also a tool of power—removing a man from his post or rewarding him with the king's personal attention. The phrase 'wash your feet,' as The Covenant Rendering notes, reflects actual ancient custom: feet became dusty and sore from travel, and washing them was associated with rest, refreshment, and the comforts of home (Genesis 18:4, 19:2). David's invitation to 'wash your feet' would have sounded entirely natural to Uriah as a hospitable command to rest after his journey.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: The pattern of a leader's outward courtesy masking inward corruption finds a parallel in Alma 8:9-10, where the people of Ammonihah receive Alma civilly but have already hardened their hearts against his message. Outward greeting conceals inward opposition.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 121:39 teaches that 'it is the nature and disposition of almost all men, as soon as they get a little authority...they will immediately begin to exercise unrighteous dominion.' David's use of his royal authority to manipulate Uriah exemplifies this principle—he wields his power not to serve but to gratify and conceal.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The repeated language of shalom connects to the temple covenant, where peace is promised to those who keep the covenants. David's false inquiry about shalom while breaking covenant represents a profound violation of the sacred order he is meant to uphold.

commentary.christological_typology: David's false inquiry about welfare, concealing a plot against an innocent man, stands in stark contrast to Christ's genuine concern for His sheep. Where David asks about shalom to deceive, Christ offers true peace (John 14:27) through transparent love and willing sacrifice. The contrast between David's hidden motive and Christ's open heart reveals the distance between human kingship corrupted by power and divine kingship perfected in service.
commentary.application: This verse invites us to examine the difference between speaking the language of faith and living it. How often do we offer greetings and inquiries that feel genuine but mask self-interest? David uses the language of shalom—peace, welfare, wholeness—while his heart is bent on deception. Modern disciples are called to radical authenticity: let your yes be yes, let your concern for others flow from genuine love rather than hidden agenda. The warning here is personal: the person who can ask 'How are you?' while plotting harm against you is someone we may not yet see clearly. More importantly, we must examine ourselves: are we asking questions we genuinely care about, or performing concern?

text_kjv: And David said to Uriah, Go down to thine house, and wash thy feet. And Uriah departed out of the king's house, and there followed him a mess of meat from the king.

commentary.narrative:
David's command is phrased as a gracious invitation: go home, rest, refresh yourself. 'Wash your feet' is an idiom for relaxation after travel—a comfortable stay at home with all its domestic pleasures. The phrase carries an implicit understanding in Hebrew culture: a man who goes home to wash his feet will naturally spend the evening with his wife. David is not ordering Uriah to sin; he is creating a scenario in which normal, honorable conjugal relations will occur—and in which the paternity of Bathsheba's child can plausibly be attributed to Uriah rather than the king.

The narrator adds a detail that reveals David's calculated generosity: a royal gift of food and wine is sent after Uriah. This is not mere kindness. As The Covenant Rendering emphasizes, it is an inducement, sweetening the homecoming and making refusal seem churlish. David is buying Uriah's compliance with comfort and honor. The grotesque irony is that the king sends a royal gift to a man he is secretly determined to destroy. The narrative voice remains neutral—it simply reports what was sent and that it followed Uriah—but the reader begins to feel the weight of the king's manipulation: every gesture of kindness is a tool, every gift a weapon.

word_study.meaning: to go down, descend; can be literal (going downhill) or figurative (going down to a place, going to rest or sleep). In biblical idiom, 'going down' to one's house often implies returning home for rest.
word_study.significance: David's command red le-veitekha ('go down to your house') is a gentle, almost paternal directive. The verb will be echoed and negated repeatedly—Uriah 'did not go down'—making the refusal unmistakable. The word itself becomes a pivot point in the narrative.

word_study.meaning: to wash, bathe, cleanse. In context, washing the feet after travel was a common act of refreshment and a preparation for rest and domestic enjoyment.
word_study.significance: The act of washing feet appears throughout scripture as an act of hospitality and care (Genesis 18:4, 19:2, John 13:5). Here it is weaponized—used euphemistically to invite Uriah into a situation where David intends to exploit him.

word_study.meaning: a portion, gift, or share; mas'at ha-melekh specifically means a royal portion or gift sent by the king, often of food or wine. The word carries the sense of something lifted up or exalted, something given as a mark of honor.
word_study.significance: The royal gift is presented without explanation—it simply 'was sent after him.' The narrator's restraint here is masterful: he does not editorialze, but lets the reader feel the disparity between royal generosity and royal treachery.

cross_references.connection: When Lot offers hospitality to the angels, he says 'I pray you...wash your feet'—the same language David uses, showing that the idiom was conventional for inviting rest and domestic comfort.

When Jesse sends David to Saul's court, he sends 'a present'—mas'at—along with him, showing that royal gifts were customary tokens of honor and favor, making David's gift to Uriah seem innocent on the surface.
The proverb teaches that 'a man's gift maketh room for him...before great men,' suggesting that gifts are tools of influence—exactly David's strategy with Uriah.
Nathan's parable will later expose this very dynamic: the rich man taking the poor man's ewe lamb, offering a gift while planning destruction—a mirror of David's false generosity to Uriah.
The Book of Mormon warns against those who 'lay wait to catch us'—those who offer kindness as a tool of entrapment, exactly as David does here.

commentary.historical_context: In ancient Near Eastern royal courts, a monarch's personal invitation to rest and the sending of a royal portion were genuine honors. For a soldier to refuse such an invitation would have been deeply insulting—a breach of protocol and gratitude. David's command to 'go down to your house and wash your feet' followed by a royal gift would have been received by Uriah as an extraordinary honor: the king personally concerned with his comfort, the palace kitchen providing for his meal. The cultural context makes Uriah's subsequent refusal even more striking—he will violate protocol, reject honor, and risk the king's displeasure because something deeper calls him. The 'mess of meat' (mas'at) was likely bread, meat, and wine, the elements of a celebratory meal. In ancient Israelite custom, sharing food with someone was a covenant act, binding the parties together. David's gift would have been understood as a sign of the king's favor and Uriah's acceptance into the inner circle.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: Jacob 7:2-5 describes Sherem coming to Jacob with soft words and flattery, seeking to lead him astray—much as David uses gentle language and royal gifts to manipulate Uriah. The tools of seduction are often courteous and appealing.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 50:23 teaches that 'that which is of God is light; and he that receiveth light...receiveth light.' David's manipulation, by contrast, operates in darkness—his words speak of care while his heart intends harm. The contrast illuminates what it means to walk in light.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The washing of feet in temple ordinance represents cleansing and preparation for sacred covenants. David corrupts this symbolism, using the language of preparation and cleansing to set a trap. True washing leads to covenant faithfulness; David's invitation leads to covenant-breaking.

commentary.christological_typology: Christ washed the feet of His disciples (John 13:4-5) as an act of humble service, establishing the pattern of true leadership. David washes a man's feet (invites him to wash) as a tool of manipulation. The contrast reveals the difference between leadership that serves and leadership that exploits, between power that empowers and power that enslaves.
commentary.application: We live in a world of subtle manipulation—where gifts come with hidden strings, where kindness is sometimes strategic, where hospitality can mask ulterior motive. This verse calls us to discern the difference between genuine generosity and manipulation masquerading as care. On the receiving end, we must ask: What is the cost of accepting this gift? What does the giver expect in return? On the giving end, we must examine our own hearts: Am I being generous because I truly care, or am I trying to influence someone toward a goal they would reject if they knew my motive? True Christian hospitality, like Christ's foot-washing, asks nothing in return and manipulates no one.

text_kjv: But Uriah slept at the door of the king's house with all the servants of his lord, and went not down to his house.

commentary.narrative:
This verse is the hammer blow that shatters David's plan. Uriah, having been graciously dismissed to his home with a royal gift, does not go home. Instead, he sleeps at the entrance of the palace with the other royal servants. The verb 'went not down' (lo yarad) is the direct negation of David's command 'go down' (red le-veitekha) from verse 8. The narrator's restraint is absolute: he provides no explanation of Uriah's motive, no access to his reasoning. He simply states the fact with devastating clarity: Uriah did not go down.

This refusal is an act of extraordinary integrity that the narrative does not yet explain. The reader is left to wonder why any man, especially one granted a royal dismissal and a royal gift, would sleep at the palace entrance rather than go home to his own bed and his own wife. The answer will come in verse 11, where Uriah himself will articulate his reasoning—and it will be rooted in something deeper than the king's shallow manipulation. The Covenant Rendering notes that by sleeping with the royal servants, Uriah demonstrates solidarity with the common soldiers: if the army is in the field, the soldier will share their hardship. The phrase 'with all the servants of his lord' emphasizes Uriah's identification with the troops rather than with comfort.

word_study.meaning: to lie down, sleep, recline. The word can be neutral or can carry sexual implication depending on context (e.g., 'lay with').
word_study.significance: The verb shakab is carefully controlled here—it describes innocent sleep, not conjugal relations. The next verse will use the same verb again (verse 11), where Uriah explicitly refuses to 'lie with' (shakab im) his wife. The repetition of the verb with different objects—sleep at the palace, but not with his wife—underscores his refusal.

word_study.meaning: door, entrance, gateway; metaphorically, the threshold or boundary between spaces.
word_study.significance: Uriah sleeps at the petach beit ha-melekh—the entrance of the king's house—not inside the palace where comfort awaited. The spatial detail is important: he is at the threshold, not within. He maintains a kind of separation, a refusal to fully enter into the king's world of ease.

word_study.meaning: did not descend, did not go down; the negation of the verb yarad, 'to go down'
word_study.significance: This phrase becomes a refrain in the narrative: 'Uriah went not down' (verse 9), 'Uriah did not go down' (verse 10, in David's question), and 'He did not go down' (in the report to David). The repetition of the negation builds pressure in the narrative, emphasizing Uriah's refusal with each iteration.

cross_references.connection: When Saul urges the woman at Endor to prepare food for him after consulting the spirit, his servants 'also urge him'—showing that following a direct command from authority was the normal expectation, making Uriah's refusal even more remarkable.

The law stipulates that men in an army must maintain ritual purity and avoid defilement, requiring separation from the camp during certain conditions—Uriah's refusal to enjoy comfort while the army camps in the field may reflect this covenantal consciousness.
Paul teaches that eating and drinking unworthily 'eateth and drinketh damnation to himself'—Uriah refuses to eat and drink in comfort because his conscience forbids it while others suffer.

When David later flees Jerusalem in shame, he 'went up...with his head covered, and...wept' and his followers wept—the contrast with his current position of power shows how quickly a king can be humbled.

cross_references.reference: Nephi's refusal of the kingdom of Lehi
cross_references.connection: Uriah's refusal to enjoy privilege while his brothers (the soldiers) suffer in the field parallels Nephi's refusal to be made king (Jacob 1:11), both men choosing solidarity with the righteous over personal comfort.

commentary.historical_context: In ancient Near Eastern military culture, the bond between a commander and his troops was sacred. A soldier's loyalty to his unit and to his comrades often superseded other loyalties. The practice of sleeping in the barracks with one's fellows was a sign of military discipline and unit cohesion—a Hittite (Uriah's nationality) would have been especially conscious of these bonds. The fact that Uriah chooses to sleep at the palace entrance with the royal servants rather than going home suggests he views his duty to the army as binding even while he is away from the battlefield. The palace entrance would have been a public space, perhaps with a courtyard where servants and soldiers rested. By sleeping there, Uriah makes a public statement: I am a soldier first, and my place is with my brothers in arms, not at ease in my own home.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: Helaman 1:13-15 describes soldiers who refused to abandon their positions or enjoy comfort while their comrades were in danger—the same covenantal consciousness Uriah displays. Alma 48:11-13 praises the soldiers of Helaman for their devotion to righteousness and to one another, much as Uriah demonstrates here.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 38:27 teaches that 'all things must be done in order' and according to covenantal law. Uriah, though he may not have had explicit revelation, acts according to a deep covenantal consciousness—the Ark is in the field, the soldiers are in danger, and he will not abandon them for comfort.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: Temple covenants involve the principle of sacrifice—of laying down personal comfort and desire for a higher cause. Uriah's refusal to enjoy comfort while others sacrifice is a form of personal sacrifice and covenant loyalty, demonstrating the principle of the temple without having received the explicit ordinances.

commentary.christological_typology: Christ's refusal to abandon His mission for personal comfort (Matthew 26:39) parallels Uriah's refusal to abandon his soldiers for the comfort of home. Both men prioritize fidelity to a higher calling over personal ease. The contrast between the king who seeks comfort and the soldier who refuses it prefigures the King of Kings who emptied Himself of all comfort and privilege.
commentary.application: Uriah's silent refusal invites us to examine our own priorities. When we are offered comfort or advancement, do we stop to consider the cost to others? When we are invited to step away from our responsibilities, do we have the courage to say no—not with words, but with our presence? The power of Uriah's refusal is that it is wordless and public. He does not announce his conscience; he simply does not go home. He is present with the servants, sleeping at the entrance of the palace, making his statement through his body. In our own lives, our presence and absence communicate volumes. Where we choose to be, whom we choose to be with, and what comforts we accept or refuse all speak to our true allegiances.

text_kjv: And when they had told David, saying, Uriah went not down unto his house, David said unto Uriah, Camest thou not from thy journey? why then didst thou not go down unto thine house?

commentary.narrative:
David's plan has failed, and his response is to confront Uriah with a show of bewilderment and paternal concern. The king asks why any man, fresh from a long journey, would not go home to rest. The question is framed as reasonable: Surely you must be tired? Why not enjoy the comfort of your own house? But beneath the surface reasonableness lies desperation. David has already discovered that Uriah did not comply with his gracious dismissal, and now he is trying a different approach—not command, but persuasion; not flattery, but the appeal to common sense.

The double use of the verb 'go down' (yarad) in this verse—first in the report 'Uriah went not down' and then in David's question 'why didst thou not go down'—creates a verbal echo that hammers on the point of Uriah's refusal. David himself becomes the messenger of his own failure: by asking the question, he highlights the very refusal he is trying to overcome. The Covenant Rendering notes that David's tone is 'casual, almost fatherly,' but the reader senses the calculation beneath it. David cannot order Uriah to disobey his conscience (though he will try different tactics in verse 13), so he appeals to normalcy: What man would refuse such obvious comfort?

word_study.meaning: to tell, report, announce, make known; to reveal or declare information to someone
word_study.significance: The passive 'they had told David' suggests that Uriah's refusal was notable enough to be reported—it was not a subtle rejection but obvious enough to come to the king's attention, raising questions.

word_study.term_original: הֲלוֹא מִדֶּרֶךְ אַתָּה בָא (ha-lo mi-derekh attah ba)
word_study.meaning: Haven't you come from a journey/road? The phrase uses the interrogative ha-lo ('not?') in a rhetorical question designed to elicit agreement.
word_study.significance: David's question is rhetorically crafted to be unanswerable—of course Uriah came from a journey; the king knows this. The rhetorical structure is manipulative: it assumes Uriah's agreement and builds to the conclusion that he therefore 'should' have gone home.

word_study.meaning: road, way, journey, path; also used metaphorically for conduct or manner of life
word_study.significance: David refers to Uriah's travel from the battlefield as a 'derekh' (journey/road), emphasizing the physical exertion and weariness Uriah should naturally want to recover from. The word is literal but chosen to reinforce David's appeal to comfort.

cross_references.connection: Abraham's hospitality to the travelers contrasts with David's false concern—Abraham asks his guests to rest, genuinely wanting their comfort, while David asks only to manipulate them.
The proverb teaches that 'He that hateth dissembleth with his lips, and layeth up deceit within him'—David's apparently reasonable questions mask his inward conspiracy against Uriah.
Judas greets Jesus with a kiss—a sign of affection masking betrayal. David addresses Uriah with seemingly reasonable concern, masking his determination to destroy him.

David will later judge the rich man in Nathan's parable harshly, saying 'he shall restore the lamb fourfold'—yet David himself is the rich man, and his manipulation of Uriah is far worse than simple theft.

Alma warns that 'wickedness never was happiness,' and the wicked labor 'anxiously that they might accomplish their designs'—David's growing desperation to make his plan work illustrates this principle.

commentary.historical_context: In the ancient Near Eastern court, a king's direct question to a subject was effectively a command, even if phrased as an inquiry. When David asks 'Why did you not go down to your house?', he is not asking for information—he is expressing displeasure and demanding an explanation. The form of the question is deferential (it allows Uriah to respond), but the substance is coercive. A subject who refused a direct royal inquiry without justification risked losing favor or facing punishment. This makes Uriah's forthcoming answer (verse 11) even more extraordinary: he will directly refuse the king's implicit command, and he will do so not by arguing with the king but by articulating a principle that stands above royal authority.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: Alma 12:9-11 teaches that 'all things which have been revealed unto the children of men shall at last be made known unto them'—David's hidden plan is about to be exposed by Uriah's refusal and, ultimately, by Nathan's prophecy.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 121:43 teaches that leaders should govern 'by persuasion, by long-suffering, by gentleness and meekness, and by love unfeigned.' David attempts persuasion, but it is feigned love, and it is aimed at manipulating Uriah into compromise.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The temple covenant calls individuals to walk in the light and to refuse deception. David's question, though on its surface reasonable, is fundamentally dishonest—it appeals to weariness and comfort while concealing a plot. Uriah will answer by appealing to a higher covenant.

commentary.christological_typology: Christ faced questions designed to entrap Him (Matthew 22:15-22), yet He answered with wisdom and truth. David's question is designed to manipulate Uriah toward sin. The contrast shows the difference between questions asked to guide toward truth and questions asked to seduce toward evil.
commentary.application: This verse teaches us to discern manipulation dressed as concern. When someone asks you a reasonable-sounding question about your own comfort or advancement, pause and ask: What is the hidden agenda behind this question? Whose interest is truly being served? David's question 'Haven't you just come from a journey?' seems to express genuine care, but it is a Trojan horse concealing a demand. We are called to cultivate Uriah's ability to sense when we are being pressured toward something that violates our deeper conscience—and to have the courage to refuse, even when refusal means disappointing someone in authority.

text_kjv: And Uriah said unto David, The ark, and Israel, and Judah, abide in tents; and my lord Joab, and the servants of my lord, are encamped in the open fields; shall I then go into mine house, to eat and to drink, and to lie with my wife? as thou livest, and as thy soul liveth, I will not do this thing.

commentary.narrative:
Uriah's response is the moral center of this passage. He speaks to David with respect (he addresses him as 'my lord'), yet his answer is a complete refusal—couched not in defiance but in principle. Uriah names the Ark of the Covenant first in his list of what is displaced by war: 'The ark, and Israel, and Judah, abide in tents.' This is the theological breakthrough. A Hittite soldier—a foreigner, a man outside the covenant people—understands something about the Ark and its significance that the anointed king of Israel has forgotten.

The Covenant Rendering emphasizes the radical implication: the Ark represents the presence of God with His people. If the Ark is in a field shelter exposed to the elements, then God Himself is enduring the hardship of war alongside the troops. How, then, can Uriah abandon the army to enjoy the comforts of home? The logic is covenantal: solidarity with God requires solidarity with God's people. Uriah's refusal becomes a form of worship—an implicit declaration that the covenantal bond is more important than personal comfort. The escalation in his statement is worth noting: from the Ark and the nation to his commander Joab to the royal servants. Everything is in the field; everything is at risk. Uriah's concluding oath—'as thou livest, and as thy soul liveth, I will not do this thing'—is the strongest available Hebrew oath, sworn upon the life of the person addressed. Uriah swears on David's own life that he will not do what David needs him to do.

word_study.meaning: ark, chest, or box; specifically, the Ark of the Covenant, the most sacred object in Israel, understood as the earthly throne of God and the visible symbol of the divine presence
