In ancient royal narratives, the king's power is often defined by his ability to defeat and eliminate rivals. Solomon's refusal to ask for this reveals that he does not seek power defined by domination over enemies but by justice toward the people he serves.

word_study.meaning: Understanding to hear/listen to justice, discernment to perceive judgment. God restates Solomon's request using slightly different language: he asks for havin (analytical understanding, the ability to perceive) to lishmo'a (to hear, to listen to) mishpat (justice, judgment, legal decision).
word_study.significance: God's restatement emphasizes the auditory and perceptive dimension. Solomon is asking for the capacity to hear what justice demands in particular situations, not merely to apply abstract rules. This confirms that the listening posture Solomon requested is indeed what God understood him to be asking for.

word_study.meaning: To/for you, yourself. The preposition-suffix lekha indicates possession or benefit accruing to the person addressed.
word_study.significance: God's triple repetition of lekha ('for yourself, for your own benefit') — emphasizing what Solomon did not ask for himself — highlights that Solomon's singular request was for something that would benefit the people, not the king. This self-abnegation is what moved God.

cross_references.connection: Moses presents Israel with a choice: 'I have set before you life and good, and death and evil... Therefore choose life, that thou and thy seed may live.' Solomon's choice to ask for the capacity to do good (through wise judgment) rather than seeking personal advantage mirrors this pattern of choosing life and good over self-serving alternatives.

Later attributed to Solomon: 'For wisdom is better than rubies; and all the things that may be desired are not to be compared to it.' This proverb reflects Solomon's own discovery in this chapter: wisdom is more valuable than wealth, longevity, or power — because wisdom enables all the genuine goods that wealth or power merely imitate.

Jesus teaches: 'Take no thought for your life, what ye shall eat... But seek ye first the kingdom of God, and his righteousness; and all these things shall be added unto you.' Solomon models this principle: by not asking for security, wealth, or power, he positions himself to receive all of them as overflow from the central gift of wisdom.

Peter writes: 'God resisteth the proud, but giveth grace unto the humble... Humble yourselves therefore under the mighty hand of God, that he may exalt you in due time.' Solomon's humble petition — focusing on the good of others rather than his own advantage — demonstrates the humility that precedes exaltation.

The Lord tells Church leaders that dominion cannot be exercised 'by virtue of the priesthood' through 'persuasion, by long-suffering, by gentleness and meekness, and by love unfeigned.' Solomon's request for wisdom to judge justly rather than for power to dominate aligns with this Restoration principle.

commentary.historical_context: God's enumeration of what Solomon did not ask for reveals the typical concerns of ancient kings. In Egyptian royal texts, pharaohs emphasize their long reign and accumulated wealth as signs of divine favor. In Mesopotamian chronicles, kings boast of military victories and the destruction of enemies. Solomon's refusal to prioritize these goods marks him as operating within a different value system — the covenant framework in which a king's role is to embody God's justice, not to accumulate personal advantage. The fact that God explicitly approves this prioritization (by contrasting it with typical royal petitions) suggests that the covenant ideology of kingship — the king as God's servant to the people, not God's tool for his own purposes — is being affirmed as the true model.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: In Alma 29:10-11, Alma the Younger uses language strikingly similar to God's enumeration in this verse: 'But behold, I am a man, and do sin in my wish... I ought not to harass and wear out the hands of my brethren... I ought to be content with the things which the Lord hath allotted unto me.' Alma learns what Solomon practiced: the refusal to wish for things outside one's sphere of service, the contentment with one's role as it is defined by the Lord.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 11:20 states: 'Seek not for riches but for wisdom, and behold, the mysteries of God shall be unfolded unto you, and then shall you be made rich.' This direct parallel to Solomon's experience articulates the Restoration principle: when you seek wisdom (the true priority) rather than riches, both wisdom and abundance follow. D&C 84:85 teaches: 'That the preaching of the gospel may be continued in the season thereof, and that souls may be gathered out.' The focus is on gathering souls, not accumulating wealth — the same reorientation Solomon made in his prayer.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: Solomon's choice to seek understanding for justice rather than personal power is the foundation for the temple he will build. The temple, like the kingdom of God in all times, exists not for the king's glory but for the people's covenant relationship with God. Solomon's prayer establishes that he understands this theological priority, making him the appropriate builder of God's house.

commentary.christological_typology: Christ embodies the principle demonstrated by Solomon's refusal to ask for personal advantage. In the wilderness temptations (Matthew 4:1-11), Satan offers Jesus kingdoms, food (wealth and security), and power. Jesus refuses all of them — not asking God to provide these things for His own comfort or dominion. Instead, He focuses entirely on accomplishing the Father's purposes. At Gethsemane, Jesus prays: 'Not my will, but thine, be done' (Luke 22:42), enacting Solomon's principle of subordinating personal desire to the greater good. Like Solomon, Christ is exalted not despite this refusal to prioritize personal advantage but because of it. Hebrews 2:9 states: 'But we see Jesus, who was made a little lower than the angels for the suffering of death, crowned with glory and honour.' The pattern is consistent across Scripture: those who refuse to seek power and advantage for themselves are those whom God exalts.
commentary.application: This verse operates as a mirror for believers to examine their own prayer lives. What do we ask God for? The truth is that our petitions reveal our deepest priorities. If our prayers focus on job security, financial abundance, freedom from enemies or obstacles, or extended life and health for ourselves, that is not sin — these are legitimate human concerns. But God's approval seems to attend a different category of petition: prayers for capacity to serve others well, for wisdom to judge justly, for the strength to love sacrificially. This verse suggests that the prayers most likely to align us with God's character are those where we ask Him to give us the capacity to serve others, even at cost to ourselves. A parent might pray not 'let my child succeed in worldly terms' but 'give me understanding to know what my child truly needs.' A spouse might pray not 'make my marriage easy' but 'give me the listening heart to understand my partner.' A professional might pray not 'let me advance' but 'let me discern the right action in this complex situation, regardless of how it affects my career.' These prayers — focused on others' good rather than our own advantage — are the prayers that most closely resemble Solomon's, and they are the prayers most likely to receive God's approval and answer.

text_kjv: Behold, I have done according to thy words: lo, I have given thee a wise and an understanding heart; so that there was none like thee before thee, neither after thee shall any arise like unto thee.

commentary.narrative:
God's response moves from approving Solomon's request to granting it in superlative terms. The verb 'done according to thy words' (asiti kidvarekha in Hebrew) indicates that God is fulfilling Solomon's petition with precision — Solomon asked, and God delivers exactly what was asked for, but amplified beyond measure. The phrase 'I have given thee' (natatti lekha) marks the moment of transmission: the gift is now Solomon's possession. But what God gives is not merely what Solomon asked for; it is something greater.

Solomon asked for a 'listening heart' (lev shomea) to judge his people. God grants him a 'wise and discerning heart' (lev chakham venavon). The Covenant Rendering captures the distinction: Solomon asked for listening capacity, and God gives him wisdom and discernment — the fuller realization of what listening makes possible. Chokmah ('wisdom') is not abstract knowledge but the skilled ability to navigate reality rightly, to see through deception, to render decisions that restore order. Navon ('discerning') from the root bin indicates analytical perception — the ability to perceive distinctions, to see through surfaces to underlying truths. Together, they represent complete intellectual and moral equipment for governance.

Then comes the extraordinary declaration: 'so that there was none like thee before thee, neither after thee shall any arise like unto thee.' This is absolute language. God is not saying Solomon will be among the wisest, or the most famous, or the greatest of a generation. He is saying that Solomon's wisdom is historically unique — unmatched in the past and unrepeatable in the future. The verb yaqum ('shall arise') suggests that wise figures may appear in future ages, but none will rise to Solomon's level. This makes Solomon's wisdom not merely a personal gift but a historical singularity, a one-time divine endowment without parallel. The reader understands that Solomon has received not just an answer to his prayer but a superlative gift that establishes him as the pinnacle of human wisdom in the biblical timeline.

word_study.meaning: I have done according to your words, I have fulfilled your petition. The verb asah ('to do, to make, to perform') in the qal perfect indicates completed action. The preposition ki-dvarekha ('according to your words') shows that God's action is responsive to Solomon's petition.
word_study.significance: God presents His gift-giving as a direct response to Solomon's request. This emphasizes that Solomon's petition was heard and understood, and that God is granting what was asked for.

word_study.meaning: I have given to you, I have bestowed upon you. The verb natan in the qal perfect with the preposition le ('to, for') indicates the transfer of possession.
word_study.significance: This is the moment of the gift's transmission. The wisdom is now Solomon's to possess and employ. The gift is not merely promised but actually transferred.

word_study.meaning: Wisdom, skillfulness, the ability to act rightly. In Hebrew, chokmah is not abstract philosophical knowledge but the applied intelligence to navigate situations skillfully. A chakham ('wise person') is someone who knows how things work and acts accordingly, whether as an artisan, administrator, judge, or leader.
word_study.significance: God names chokmah as the primary gift. Solomon asked for a listening heart; God grants the wisdom that such listening makes possible. Wisdom is the ability to perceive what listening reveals and to act accordingly.

word_study.meaning: Discerning, understanding, perceiving. The adjective navon derives from the verb bin ('to understand, to perceive, to have insight'). A navon person is one who perceives distinctions, who analyzes, who sees through surfaces to underlying realities.
word_study.significance: This adds a dimension beyond chokmah alone. While chokmah is the ability to act skillfully, navon is the perception that enables such skill. Together, chokmah and navon represent complete intellectual and moral equipment: the ability to see truly and the ability to act wisely based on what is seen.

word_study.term_original: אֲשֶׁר כָּמוֹךָ לֹא־הָיָה לְפָנֶיךָ (asher kamokha lo hayah lefanekha)
word_study.meaning: Such that no one like you has existed before you. The phrase uses a negative comparative structure: 'one like you did not exist in front of you' (where 'in front of you' means 'before you' in time).
word_study.significance: This brackets Solomon's wisdom as historically unprecedented. No one before Solomon, despite centuries of history and multiple generations of leaders, has achieved his level of wisdom.

word_study.term_english: neither after thee shall any arise like unto thee
word_study.term_original: וְאַחֲרֶיךָ לֹא־יָקוּם כָּמוֹךָ (veacharekha lo yaqum kamokha)
word_study.meaning: And after you, no one like you will arise. The verb yaqum ('shall arise, shall stand up') suggests that future figures may appear, but none will rise to Solomon's level of wisdom.
word_study.significance: This extends the uniqueness forward into all future history. Solomon is not merely the wisest of his age; he is the wisest that anyone will ever be. The superlative applies to all of human history, past and future.

cross_references.connection: Later attributed to Solomon: 'Happy is the man that findeth wisdom, and the man that getteth understanding... She is more precious than rubies; and all the things thou canst desire are not to be compared unto her.' These verses reflect Solomon's own experience in 1 Kings 3: wisdom is the supreme good, more valuable than any other possession.

The text later reports: 'God gave Solomon wisdom and understanding exceeding much, and largeness of heart, even as the sand that is on the sea shore... And Solomon's wisdom excelled the wisdom of all the children of the east country... And there came of all people to hear the wisdom of Solomon.' This narrative expansion demonstrates the practical outworking of the gift granted in verse 12.

The Queen of Sheba visits Solomon to 'prove him with hard questions... And Solomon told her all her questions: there was not any thing hid from the king, which he told her not.' The narrative demonstrates Solomon's wisdom in action — his ability to perceive and answer complex questions reflects the listening and discerning heart God granted.

Solomon later reflects: 'I have acquired great wisdom and knowledge, surpassing all who were before me.' If this is indeed Solomon's reflective work in old age, he is recalling the gift granted in this moment and meditating on its meaning.

The epistle states that Christ is 'made so much better than the angels, as he hath by inheritance obtained a more excellent name than they.' Like Solomon, Christ is presented as superlatively exalted — not merely great but uniquely so — and this exaltation is the result of having prioritized the Father's purposes over His own advantage.

commentary.historical_context: Solomon's reign (traditionally dated to ca. 970-930 BCE, though scholarly debate continues) was remembered in Israelite tradition as an era of unprecedented prosperity, cultural achievement, and international prominence. While modern archaeology has questioned whether Solomon's kingdom was as expansive as the biblical record suggests, the literary tradition consistently portrays his era as the apex of Israel's pre-exile history. His wisdom became legendary throughout the ancient Near East; the visit of the Queen of Sheba (1 Kings 10) exemplifies how Solomon's fame spread to distant lands. The portrayal of Solomon as the wisest of all people served a theological purpose in the biblical narrative: it established the reign of David and Solomon as Israel's golden age, the period when the kingdom of God was most fully realized in history. This made the subsequent division of the kingdom (1 Kings 12) and the eventual exile all the more poignant — Israel had fallen from this unprecedented high point.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: In Mosiah 8:16-18, King Limhi describes a man who can interpret engravings by the gift of the Spirit: 'Now the king said that a seer is greater than a prophet... Yea, and a seer can know of things which are past, and also of things which are to come.' The superlative language used of Solomon — that no one like him shall arise — appears also in Book of Mormon accounts of those endowed with extraordinary spiritual gifts. Similarly, Alma is described as having received a visitation from an angel and subsequent knowledge that exceeds that of others.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 124:34 states: 'I have appointed you, and not because of your own righteousness... that you might be exalted.' The pattern is that God grants extraordinary gifts to those who prioritize His purposes. D&C 76:70 describes those who inherit the celestial kingdom as receiving 'all things' after they have been 'made perfect.' Solomon's receipt of wisdom exceeding all others reflects the principle that those who surrender personal advantage receive divine gifts that exceed all expectation.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: Solomon's wisdom is the essential qualification for his role in building the temple. A temple requires not merely physical construction but spiritual understanding — knowing how to embody God's presence, how to structure space to facilitate covenant, how to design systems that direct the people's hearts toward God. Solomon's superlative wisdom enables him to accomplish this at a level that subsequent temple builders (in the post-exile rebuilding or in Herod's expansion) could not match. The temple built during Solomon's reign becomes the paradigm for all subsequent temples in Israel's history.

commentary.christological_typology: The declaration that Solomon has received a wisdom 'so that there was none like thee before thee, neither after thee shall any arise like unto thee' foreshadows in a lesser key the unique exaltation of Christ. In Colossians 1:15-19, Paul describes Christ as 'the image of the invisible God, the firstborn of every creature: For by him were all things created... he is the head of the body, the church: who is the beginning, the firstborn from the dead; that in all things he might have the preeminence.' Where Solomon is supremely wise, Christ is the incarnate Wisdom of God (1 Corinthians 1:24). Where Solomon's wisdom is granted to him and is therefore derived, Christ's wisdom is intrinsic and eternal — 'In him are hid all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge' (Colossians 2:3). Solomon's superlative wisdom points toward but pales in comparison to the absolute wisdom that is Christ Himself.
commentary.application: This final verse of the passage operates on multiple levels for modern readers. First, it models the principle that extraordinary capacity comes to those who prioritize others' good over their own. Solomon did not ask for greatness; he asked for the capacity to serve his people justly. The greatness came as an overflow of that right priority. Second, it teaches the nature of true wisdom. Wisdom is not accumulation of information, not mastery of abstract theory, not intellectual pride. Wisdom is the capacity to perceive what is true and to act accordingly — to see through the deceptions that entrap less discerning people, to understand what a particular situation demands, to render decisions that restore order and justice. This kind of wisdom is available to all believers who, like Solomon, approach God acknowledging their inadequacy and asking for a listening heart to discern rightly. Third, it reminds us that the gifts God grants exceed what we ask for. Solomon asked for one thing; God gave him that thing and more. The promise is not merely that God will answer our prayers but that His answers overflow our expectations. Finally, the verse assures us that wisdom is the supremely valuable gift. In a world that often measures worth by wealth, power, or prestige, Solomon's example and God's affirmation establish that wisdom — the capacity to perceive truly and act rightly — is more precious than all other goods. A person of wisdom can navigate life successfully; a person of wisdom can help others flourish; a person of wisdom can leave a legacy that endures. This should reshape our prayer lives and our priorities in the direction Solomon modeled.

text_kjv: And I have also given thee that which thou hast not asked, both riches, and honour: so that there shall not be any among the kings like unto thee all thy days.

commentary.narrative:
God's response to Solomon's selfless request reveals a fundamental principle of divine economy: what you do not ask for, God gives freely. Solomon asked only for wisdom to judge God's people rightly—a request focused entirely on his covenant responsibility, not his personal advancement. God honors this restraint by granting not only the requested wisdom but also wealth (osher) and honor (kavod) that Solomon never sought. This is the inverse of human ambition, where people typically grasp for riches and status and hope wisdom follows. The divine principle inverts the order: seek first the kingdom and righteousness, and all these things will be added to you (Matthew 6:33).

The phrase "that there shall not be any among the kings like unto thee all thy days" establishes Solomon's unequaled position in history—not through his own striving but through God's generous overflow. The comparative structure ("no king will be your equal") emphasizes that this is not merely success but singular preeminence. The Covenant Rendering captures the nuance more sharply: "so that no king will be your equal during your entire lifetime." This temporal qualifier—"during your entire lifetime"—leaves open the possibility that this preeminence is conditional and could theoretically be forfeited. Indeed, 1 Kings 11 will demonstrate that Solomon's later choices do diminish his glory.

The connection between the "weight" (kavod, from k-v-d) of Israel's people mentioned in verse 9 and the honor now promised Solomon is theologically significant. Solomon described Israel as "a weighty people," using the same Hebrew root. The burden of stewarding such a people becomes the source of Solomon's own kavod—his honor comes not from external conquest but from the weight of covenant responsibility he faithfully bore.

word_study.meaning: wealth, riches, abundance; the root osher also means 'to be free, to become wide.' The noun carries the sense of both material abundance and spaciousness or freedom.
word_study.significance: Solomon's wealth is not presented as mere accumulation but as a broadening gift—he is given space and resources to build the Temple and extend Israel's peace and prosperity. The semantic range suggests that true wealth includes freedom and opportunity, not just possessions.

word_study.meaning: honor, glory, weight, heaviness; from the root k-v-d. Originally meant physical heaviness or weight, then transferred metaphorically to mean significance, importance, and honor. The term appears frequently in the Hebrew Bible for God's glory and human dignity.
word_study.significance: The Covenant Rendering notes the theological connection to verse 9, where Solomon used the same root describing Israel as 'am kaved' ('a weighty people'). The parallelism suggests that Solomon's honor derives from his faithful stewardship of Israel's weight—his covenant responsibility becomes his glory. This root also appears in the fourth commandment ('honor thy father and mother') and in descriptions of God's glory filling the Temple.

word_study.meaning: I have given (perfect tense); from the root n-t-n, meaning 'to give, to place, to set.'
word_study.significance: The perfect tense emphasizes that this giving is already accomplished fact from God's perspective, not future contingency. God speaks as if the gift has already been delivered, underscoring divine certainty and the irrevocable nature of the covenant promise.

cross_references.connection: Jesus teaches the principle inverted from Solomon's choice: 'Seek first the kingdom of God... and all these things shall be added unto you.' Solomon sought wisdom for God's kingdom and received riches and honor added; both demonstrate the pattern of seeking God first.

Moses warns Israel not to claim personal credit for wealth, saying 'the Lord thy God... giveth thee power to get wealth.' Like Solomon's wealth, all prosperity flows from God's faithful provision, not human merit alone.

The proverb states 'By humility and the fear of the Lord are riches, and honour, and life.' Solomon's experience exemplifies this principle—his humble request for wisdom produces both riches and honor as divinely measured rewards.
The narrator later confirms that 'Solomon exceeded all the kings of the earth for riches and for wisdom,' directly fulfilling God's promise in verse 13 that no king would be his equal.

commentary.historical_context: In the ancient Near Eastern context, royal legitimacy rested on three pillars: military power, wealth, and divine favor. Solomon's reign would become famous not for military conquest (as David's had been) but for mercantile wealth, building projects, and administrative wisdom. The cultural expectation would have been that a new king, particularly one following a warrior-king, would consolidate power through military campaigns. Solomon's choice to seek wisdom instead—and God's response by granting wealth without asking—represented a marked departure from conventional royal aspiration. The phrase about having no equal among kings reflects the ancient Near Eastern practice of royal titulature and comparison. Egyptian pharaohs and Mesopotamian kings commonly claimed preeminence; Solomon's claim is here authorized by divine decree rather than human boasting.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: In Alma 37:35, Alma teaches his son Helaman that if he 'will keep the commandments of God... the Lord shall prosper thee.' Like Solomon, Helaman is promised prosperity conditional on obedience, though the prosperity here is explicitly spiritual. The Book of Mormon repeatedly affirms that righteousness brings prosperity (Alma 50:20-21), echoing the Deuteronomic theology embedded in Solomon's covenant.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 84:38 promises that those who serve faithfully will receive grace 'and be crowned with blessings.' Solomon's unrequested blessings of wealth and honor parallel the principle that faithfulness to covenant produces unasked-for divine generosity. D&C 130:20-21 teaches the fundamental law of restoration: 'There is a law, irrevocably decreed before the foundations of this world... all blessings are predicated upon obedience.' Solomon's case demonstrates this law in action.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: Solomon's ultimate purpose, unstated here but central to his life's work, is to build the Temple—God's earthly house. The wealth and honor he receives serve that temple-building mission. His riches fund the construction (1 Kings 5-7), and his honor establishes the court and political stability necessary for the project's completion.

commentary.christological_typology: Solomon's humble request for wisdom to judge Israel prefigures Christ's role as the ultimate Judge and the source of all true wisdom. Jesus will be greater than Solomon (Matthew 12:42), embodying infinite wisdom and honor. However, where Solomon's wisdom was contingent and his honor eventually diminished by disobedience, Christ's wisdom and honor are eternal and unconditional. Hebrews 1:3 describes Christ as 'the brightness of [God's] glory'—a direct parallel to Solomon's kavod, but perfected and unchanging.
commentary.application: Solomon's experience teaches modern covenant members a counterintuitive principle: seeking first God's kingdom and righteousness produces prosperity and honor that personal ambition cannot achieve. The application is not that faithful members will become wealthy or famous—the promise is more precise than that. It is that seeking wisdom and righteousness for the right purposes (to serve others, to build God's kingdom, to fulfill covenant responsibility) removes the spiritual obstacles to prosperity. Solomon did not ask for wealth; he asked for wisdom to serve. God provided both. For modern members, the pattern suggests that ambition should focus on covenant faithfulness and service, trusting that genuine prosperity—material, relational, and spiritual—will follow. The conditional phrase "if thou wilt walk in my ways" (verse 14) reminds us that this is not a guarantee without strings; it is a promise to those who maintain their walk.

text_kjv: And if thou wilt walk in my ways, to keep my statutes and my commandments, as thy father David did walk, then I will lengthen thy days.

commentary.narrative:
This verse introduces the one gift contingent on Solomon's ongoing obedience. Whereas wisdom, wealth, and honor were granted freely in verse 13, long life is explicitly conditional. The structure of the covenant is now clarified: some promises are unconditional gifts (responding to a humble heart), while others depend on sustained faithfulness. The condition uses the language of "walking"—a covenant metaphor throughout scripture that implies an ongoing journey of alignment with God's way, not a single moment of compliance. Solomon must "walk in my ways... to keep my statutes and my commandments." The phrase echoes verse 6, where the narrator noted that Solomon's father David "walked before thee in truth." The standard for Solomon is his father's walk: not perfection, but genuine devotion with course corrections.

The verb "lengthen" (from arekh, "to be long") recalls Deuteronomic promises of long life in the land for obedience (Deuteronomy 5:33, 6:2). This is not merely personal longevity but covenant life—a life lived in the fullness of God's favor and protection. The Covenant Rendering sharpens the promise: "then I will give you a long life," emphasizing that the length itself is the gift, a quantity of years to steward and build with.

Historically, Solomon's reign would prove prosperous and lengthy (roughly 970-931 BCE, nearly forty years), but the later chapters of 1 Kings reveal the tragic trajectory. As Solomon drifted into idolatry and disobedience (particularly through foreign marriages and the tolerance of foreign gods), the spiritual foundation eroded. Though he lived out his years, the promise of verse 14 was not fully realized in the sense of continued favor and blessing. His son Rehoboam inherited a kingdom already fractured by Solomon's later disobedience. This underscores that the conditional promise, while real, requires sustained walking, not merely the memory of early faithfulness.

word_study.meaning: to walk, to go, to travel; also used metaphorically for conduct, behavior, and the trajectory of one's life. In covenant language, it describes alignment with God's way over time.
word_study.significance: The verb appears repeatedly in covenantal contexts (verse 3, verse 6, verse 14) to denote not a single act but a sustained trajectory. David 'walked before thee' (verse 6); Solomon must 'walk in my ways' (verse 14). This suggests that covenant faithfulness is measured not by isolated moments but by the overall direction and pattern of life. The Covenant Rendering's use of 'walk in my ways' preserves this metaphor more clearly than 'keep my statutes,' emphasizing the relational journey.

word_study.meaning: to keep, to guard, to observe, to watch over; implies both custody and protection. In covenantal contexts, it means to maintain, preserve, and protect the relationship through faithful adherence.
word_study.significance: The verb shamar is used for keeping God's statutes but also for God keeping His covenant. There is a reciprocal quality: Solomon keeps God's commandments; God keeps His promise. The root carries the sense of vigilant, active guarding rather than passive compliance.

word_study.meaning: to be/make long, to extend; also 'to be slow.' In the hiphil form (ha'arakhti, 'I will lengthen'), it conveys active extension—God will deliberately extend Solomon's days.
word_study.significance: This verb connects to Deuteronomic covenant theology (Deuteronomy 5:33: 'that thy days may be lengthened in the land'). Long life in the land is the prototypical reward for obedience in the Deuteronomic framework. Solomon's potential for long life is tied directly to the same obedience principle.

word_study.meaning: statutes, ordinances, decrees; from chok, meaning 'something prescribed, a boundary line.' These are divinely enacted laws, often associated with specific covenant obligations.
word_study.significance: The pairing of chukkiyim (statutes) with mitzvot (commandments) in verse 14 covers the full spectrum of covenant obligation—both the why (commandments expressing God's will) and the how (statutes as concrete practices and boundaries).

cross_references.connection: Moses tells Israel, 'Ye shall walk in all the ways which the Lord your God hath commanded you, that ye may live, and that it may be well with you, and that ye may prolong your days.' The identical promise structure—obedience leads to long life—anchors Solomon's conditional promise in covenant law.

The Deuteronomic teaching continues: 'That thou mightest fear the Lord thy God, to keep all his statutes and his commandments... that thy days may be prolonged.' Again, the connection between keeping statutes/commandments and length of days appears.

The verse references David's walking 'before thee in truth, and in righteousness, and in uprightness of heart with thee.' Solomon's mandate to walk as David walked establishes his father's life as the relational model—imperfect but genuinely devoted.

God later tells Solomon, 'Forasmuch as this is done of thee, and thou hast not kept my covenant and my statutes... I will surely rend the kingdom from thee.' The conditional promise of verse 14 is explicitly invoked and broken; Solomon's disobedience activates the consequence.

Proverbs (attributed to Solomon) teaches, 'Keep thy heart with all diligence; for out of it are the issues of life.' The verb 'keep' (shamar) echoes verse 14, now applied to internal vigilance—guarding one's heart as the source of righteous walking.

commentary.historical_context: In ancient Near Eastern royal ideology, long reign was equated with divine favor and stability. The Hittite treaties and Egyptian royal traditions present long life and dynasty continuity as rewards for vassal loyalty. Solomon's promise of lengthened days fits this cultural framework but reinterprets it through the lens of covenant law rather than mere power politics. The reference to David as the standard is significant: David was a warrior-king who made grave mistakes (Bathsheba, Uriah) yet maintained core covenantal faithfulness. David's life was 'lengthened' despite his failures because his repentance was genuine. Solomon is being invited to follow a similar pattern—not perfection, but continuous covenantal walking.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: Helaman 12:2 teaches that 'except ye shall keep the commandments... the Lord shall cause that his people shall be smited by their enemies.' The conditional nature of prosperity and preservation appears repeatedly in Book of Mormon theology. Alma 9:13 states that if people 'will repent and return unto the Lord,' they will be blessed with long life. Solomon's conditional promise parallels this principle.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 82:10 crystallizes the principle: 'There is a law, irrevocably decreed before the foundations of this world, upon which all blessings are predicated—And when we obtain any blessing from God, it is by obedience to that law upon which it is predicated.' Solomon's conditional promise of long life is predicated on the law of obedience; when he breaks the law, the condition is activated and blessings are withdrawn.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: Long life was essential for Solomon to complete the Temple project, which took approximately seven years to construct (plus time for decoration and dedication). The conditional promise ensured that if Solomon remained faithful, he would have the years necessary to see the Temple completed and dedicated. Later, his sons inherited but did not build; the temple vision was Solomon's alone. This suggests that the promise of length of days was specifically calibrated to his covenant mission.

commentary.christological_typology: Solomon's conditional promise of long life stands in contrast to Christ's eternal life, which is neither conditional nor temporally limited. However, the principle that obedience produces life echoes throughout the New Testament. John 3:36 teaches that 'he that believeth on the Son hath everlasting life.' Where Solomon's life was contingent on walking in God's ways, Christ's life and our access to it are secured through faith in Him. Yet the underlying pattern—that faithfulness to covenant produces life, while disobedience brings death—remains constant.
commentary.application: Modern covenant members face a similar structure: Some promises (like the initial covenant itself, God's love, the validity of ordinances) are unconditional gifts of grace. Others (like the fullness of blessings, the continuance of divine favor, and long life in the sense of joy and peace) depend on ongoing faithfulness. The term "walk in my ways" applies to contemporary members through their temple covenants and daily adherence to the commandments. The invitation is not perfection but direction—the overall trajectory of one's life should move toward greater alignment with God's way. Stumbles and failures do not automatically forfeit the promise if they are followed by genuine repentance and recommitment, as David's life demonstrated. The application is to examine not isolated moments but the pattern of one's walk: Does my life trajectory show alignment with God's commandments, or drift toward compromise?

text_kjv: And Solomon awoke; and, behold, it was a dream. And he came to Jerusalem, and stood before the ark of the covenant of the Lord, and offered up burnt offerings, and offered peace offerings, and made a feast for all his servants.

commentary.narrative:
The transition from divine encounter to waking moment is marked by the Hebrew particle hinneh ("behold"—look, realize, notice). Solomon awakes and recognizes that what he experienced was a dream (chalom). The recognition does not diminish the dream's authority or significance; in ancient Hebrew spirituality, divine dreams were understood as real encounters with the divine, not merely psychological phantoms. The particle hinneh signals Solomon's own realization and awakening awareness. He does not dismiss the dream or delay; his response is immediate and threefold: travel, worship, and feasting.

First, he travels to Jerusalem from Gibeon (implied by the dramatic shift in location). Gibeon was the site of the high place where God appeared to him; Jerusalem is the political and spiritual center of Israel, home to the Ark of the Covenant. His movement from the periphery to the center mirrors a spiritual orientation—he positions himself before the Ark, the physical embodiment of God's covenant presence with Israel. The verb "stood" (amad) carries the weight of formal positioning: he takes his place as king in covenant relation to the Lord.

Second, his sacrificial sequence is deliberate and theologically ordered. He offers olot (burnt offerings), which represent total consecration—the whole animal ascends in smoke to God, a gift with no human consumption. Then he offers shelamim (fellowship offerings, often translated "peace offerings"), which involve shared meals where portions go to God, portions to the priest, and portions to the worshiper—binding together heaven and earth in communion. The progression from total self-offering to communal celebration mirrors what is happening spiritually: Solomon first consecrates himself wholly to God, then extends that reconciliation into community.

Third, he makes a feast for all his servants. The word mishte (from the root shth, "to drink") carries connotations of celebration and gathering. Solomon's first public act as the newly covenant-confirmed king is to extend the joy of worship and divine favor to those under his authority. This is not personal indulgence but the diffusion of blessing throughout the kingdom. The narrator presents this sequence—worship, sacrifice, feasting—as the natural response to divine encounter.

word_study.meaning: he awoke, he woke up; from the root q-ts, meaning to awaken, to rouse, to break the spell of sleep. The verb conveys movement from unconsciousness to consciousness.
word_study.significance: The awakening is deliberate and marked by the conjunction va (and), which moves the narrative forward from the divine encounter into historical action. Solomon does not linger in the dream state but transitions immediately to action.

word_study.meaning: dream, vision during sleep; often in the Hebrew Bible a vehicle for divine communication. The term carries the assumption that dreams can be revelatory.
word_study.significance: The Covenant Rendering notes that the particle hinneh ('behold') conveys realization and surprise: Solomon recognizes that the encounter was a dream, but the recognition does not diminish its authority. In Hebrew thought, the dream is real encounter, not fantasy. This aligns with later biblical patterns where God speaks through dreams (Genesis 28:12, 37:5; 1 Samuel 28:6).

word_study.meaning: he stood before, he positioned himself in the presence of; from amad ('to stand'), lifnei ('before, in the face of'). The phrase conveys formal positioning and submission.
word_study.significance: The verb amad is used for standing before God or a king in a posture of readiness, obedience, and official capacity. It is not the stance of a worshiper in prayer but of a servant or official in duty. Solomon stands before the Ark as the Lord's appointed regent over Israel.

word_study.meaning: burnt offerings, whole offerings; from the root alah ('to go up, to ascend'). These are sacrifices where the entire animal is consumed by fire, with no portion reserved for human consumption.
word_study.significance: The olot represent total consecration and gift to God. In Solomon's context, they symbolize his complete dedication to the covenant task ahead. The root alah ('to go up') connects metaphorically to the ascent of the offering—everything goes up to God.

word_study.meaning: fellowship offerings, peace offerings, communion sacrifices; from shalom ('peace, wholeness, completeness'). These sacrifices involve shared meals where portions are reserved for God, the priest, and the worshiper.
word_study.significance: The shelamim establish communal peace and covenant fellowship. They move beyond the one-way offering (olot) to include reciprocal relationship. In the context of Solomon's newly confirmed covenant, they represent the establishment of right relationship not only with God but with the priestly community and ultimately the people.

word_study.meaning: feast, banquet, drinking celebration; from the root shth ('to drink'). The word emphasizes drinking and feasting together, often in contexts of joy, covenant, or celebration.
word_study.significance: Solomon's feast is not a private affair but a public expression. The word mishte appears elsewhere for covenant celebrations (Genesis 26:30, where Isaac and the Philistines eat and drink together in covenant). Here, Solomon shares the joy of his covenant confirmation with his servants.

cross_references.connection: Jacob dreams at Bethel and receives a divine promise; upon waking, he responds by setting up a stone and making a vow. Like Solomon, Jacob's immediate response to the dream is to mark the location and establish covenant commitment through physical action.

The Levitical law describes burnt offerings as 'a sweet savour unto the Lord.' Solomon's sacrifice follows the prescribed form, suggesting his deep familiarity with covenant law and sacrificial protocol.

The law for peace offerings describes the shared meal structure: portions for the Lord, the priest, and the worshiper. Solomon's shelamim establish this covenantal community of eating together before the Lord.

David brings the Ark to Jerusalem and 'offered burnt offerings and peace offerings before the Lord... and dealt among all the people... a cake of bread, and a good piece of flesh, and a flagon of wine.' Solomon's sacrificial response mirrors David's pattern of worship and festive generosity.

At the Temple dedication, Solomon again 'offered sacrifices before the Lord... and the same day... made a feast.' The pattern established in verse 15 repeats and escalates at the Temple dedication, suggesting that feasting and sacrifice together establish Solomon's covenantal leadership.

commentary.historical_context: The movement from Gibeon to Jerusalem represents a consolidation of religious authority. Gibeon held the tabernacle and was the primary high place early in Solomon's reign (1 Chronicles 21:29), but Jerusalem, with the Ark of the Covenant, was the true covenantal center. Solomon's journey acknowledges this shift. The sacrificial system described here follows the Levitical protocols precisely: olot (burnt offerings) and shelamim (fellowship offerings) were the two primary voluntary sacrifices, and their combined offering before the Ark would have been recognized by the priesthood as a formal covenant ceremony. The feast for servants suggests an egalitarian dimension—Solomon's joy overflows to include those under his authority, a gesture of royal generosity that would establish his reputation for justice and wisdom.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: Alma 36:22-24 describes Alma's awakening experience where he receives divine assurance; his response is to 'go forth and speak to many in the church.' Like Solomon, Alma responds to divine encounter with action oriented toward his covenant people. The Book of Mormon pattern is consistent: divine dreams and visions are not meant to produce mystical passivity but covenantal action.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 76 describes Joseph Smith's vision and concludes with the command to 'declare glad tidings unto the earth.' Similarly, the Spirit directs revelation toward action and testimony. Solomon's sacrificial response and feast for his servants demonstrate that divine gifts are meant to be channeled toward blessing others, not hoarded.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: Solomon stands before the Ark in the tabernacle at Jerusalem, the precursor to the Temple he will build. The Ark represents God's covenant presence; standing before it establishes Solomon's covenantal authority. Later, when the Temple is completed, the Ark will be moved into the Holy of Holies (1 Kings 8:6), and Solomon will again offer sacrifices in dedication (1 Kings 8:62-64). The entire trajectory of Solomon's kingship is anchored to his position before the Ark and his faithful offering of sacrifice.

commentary.christological_typology: Solomon's immediate response to divine encounter—standing before the Ark and offering sacrifice—prefigures Jesus's perfect sacrifice and His position before the Father. Hebrews 10:1-10 describes Christ's sacrifice as the ultimate fulfillment of the old sacrificial system. Where Solomon offered olot and shelamim as types, Christ offered himself once for all, an offering of complete consecration (like the olot) that established covenant peace with God and humanity (like the shelamim). The feast Solomon shares with his servants echoes the Last Supper, where Christ ate with His disciples and established covenant through shared bread and wine.
commentary.application: Modern covenant members can draw several applications from Solomon's example. First, divine encounters and confirmations should produce immediate, tangible response—not mere emotional memory but action oriented toward covenant fulfillment. If a member receives personal revelation or spiritual confirmation, the natural response should be to move toward the temple (the modern equivalent of standing before the Ark), renew covenants, and extend blessing to others. Second, sacrifice and feast go together: commitment is not private and individual but meant to build community. Sharing one's blessings—time, resources, joy—with those under one's stewardship is the natural overflow of genuine covenant renewal. Third, the sequence matters: consecration first (olot), then communion (shelamim), then celebration (feast). The order suggests that internal alignment with God's will must precede the extension of communal joy. An application in leadership is that authentic authority flows from demonstrated covenant faithfulness, not from title alone.

text_kjv: Then came there two women, that were harlots, unto the king, and stood before him.

commentary.narrative:
The transition from divine encounter to practical judgment is abrupt and deliberate. The particle az ("then, at that time") links the judgment scene directly to the promise of wisdom—this case will be the first test and demonstration of Solomon's divinely granted discernment. Two women who are described as nashim zonot (prostitutes, literally "women of harlotry") appear before the king. The narrator identifies their profession without euphemism or moral commentary; the status is relevant because it establishes their social position: these are women at the absolute bottom of Israelite society, with no husband, no male advocate, no legal standing in a patriarchal system.

That these women can come directly before the king and stand in his presence is either extraordinary desperation or extraordinary accessibility in Solomon's court—or both. In the normal course of Israelite law, women would be represented by fathers or husbands; a woman without family connections would have virtually no standing to pursue a legal claim. Yet here they are, el hammelekh ("to the king") and lefanav ("before his face, in his presence"). The narrative tests Solomon's wisdom not with a case involving nobles, priests, or wealthy landowners, but with the most marginal members of society. This is the truest test of justice: Does the king's wisdom extend to those with no power, no connections, and no advocates? The Covenant Rendering captures the finality of their position: "Then two women who were prostitutes came before the king and stood in his presence."

The verb amad ("stood") in the feminine plural indicates a formal legal posture—standing before a judge in readiness to present their case. Despite their social marginalization, they assume the stance of litigants with a right to be heard. This suggests that Solomon's reputation for justice was already known or suspected, or that legal desperation compelled them to take a step ordinarily closed to women of their status. The narrative will demonstrate that Solomon's wisdom proves adequate to distinguish truth from falsehood in a case where normal legal procedures (witnesses, male representatives, documentary evidence) are unavailable.

word_study.meaning: they came, they entered; from the root b-w-a, meaning 'to come, to enter, to go.' In the feminine plural form, it describes the movement of the two women into the king's presence.
word_study.significance: The verb taboah is used for approaching a place of judgment or authority. The women are not smuggled in secretly but come openly, petitioning the king. This suggests that access to the king's judgment seat was theoretically available even to social outcasts.

word_study.meaning: women, wives; plural of isha. The term is neutral, denoting gender and often marital or family status.
word_study.significance: The women are identified first by gender (nashim), then by their social status (zonot). The order matters: they are women first, and their marginal legal status derives from lacking the male family connections that would ordinarily define a woman's identity in patriarchal society.

word_study.meaning: prostitutes, harlots, women engaged in sexual commerce; from the root z-n-h. The term is stated factually as a social identifier, not as moral judgment by the narrator.
word_study.significance: The Covenant Rendering notes that the narrator does not moralize about the women's profession; their status simply establishes that they have no male witnesses or legal advocates. In a patriarchal legal system, they had almost no standing, which makes the king's willingness to hear their case all the more significant. The word zonah appears elsewhere in scripture for women engaged in sexual commerce (Rahab the harlot in Joshua 2) and metaphorically for Israel's unfaithfulness to the covenant (Hosea 1:2).

word_study.meaning: to the king, toward the king; the preposition el indicates direction or approach, hammelekh is the definite article + king.
word_study.significance: The women approach the king, a formal and hierarchical act. Their approach suggests both access and boldness—they are crossing social boundaries to seek justice.

word_study.meaning: and they stood; feminine plural form of amad, 'to stand.' Used of standing in a formal or official posture, often before a judge or authority.
word_study.significance: The verb amad in legal contexts denotes the formal posture of a litigant standing before a judge. The women assume this formal stance despite their marginalized status, claiming by their posture a right to be heard.

cross_references.connection: The psalmist calls judges to 'Defend the poor and fatherless: do justice to the afflicted and needy.' Solomon's willingness to hear the case of these marginalized women exemplifies this psalmist's call to judicial courage on behalf of the powerless.

Proverbs (attributed to Solomon) teaches: 'Open thy mouth for the dumb... Open thy mouth, judge righteously, and plead the cause of the poor and needy.' Solomon's action here embodies the very wisdom he later teaches—advocating for those without advocates.

Isaiah calls Israel to 'learn to do well; seek judgment, relieve the oppressed, judge the fatherless, plead for the widow.' Solomon's court becomes a place where the oppressed can plead their case, presaging this prophetic ideal.

Moses commands judges: 'Hear the causes between your brethren, and judge righteously between every man and his brother, and the stranger... Ye shall not respect persons in judgment.' Solomon's equal hearing for women at the margin of society reflects this Deuteronomic mandate.

Jesus proclaims: 'The Spirit of the Lord is upon me... to preach deliverance to the captives, and recovering of sight to the blind, to set at liberty them that are bruised.' While different in context, both Jesus and Solomon direct their power and authority toward the powerless.

commentary.historical_context: In ancient Israelite society, women occupied a subordinate legal status. A woman's legal identity was typically mediated through her father (before marriage), her husband (during marriage), or her eldest son (after widowhood). A woman outside these relational structures—especially one engaged in prostitution—would have had virtually no legal standing. The fact that two prostitutes could appear before the king suggests either that Solomon's reputation for accessible justice was already established, or that their desperation overcame normal social barriers. Some commentators suggest these women may have been residents of a royal household or servants, which would explain their access, but the text does not clarify this. What is clear is that their status as nashim zonot was unusual enough to merit narrative comment, suggesting that the case itself was remarkable—the king hearing a dispute where normal legal channels would have been closed to these women.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: Alma 41:14 teaches that justice must be administered to all: 'Therefore, all things shall be restored to their proper order, being restored by that who is the source of all things.' The Book of Mormon emphasizes that justice in God's kingdom reaches everyone, regardless of social status. King Benjamin's teachings in Mosiah 4 similarly call for care of the poor and marginalized.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 101:80 teaches that the Lord has 'declared unto you the words of the Comforter, that saith: My people... must needs be disciplined unto repentance, that they may be saved... in the presence of the Lord.' The principle is that God's justice and mercy extend to all who come before Him, not just the powerful. Solomon's court mirrors this principle—all who come before the Lord's anointed representative are to be heard.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: In the temple endowment, covenants are made before the Lord without regard to social status—all are equal before God's altar. Solomon's court, as a place where the marginalized can receive justice, reflects the temple principle that the Lord's justice is not conditioned on worldly status or power.

commentary.christological_typology: Solomon's role as a judge who hears the case of the powerless prefigures Jesus's ministry and final judgment. Jesus consistently directed His healing and teaching toward the marginalized (the woman at the well, the Canaanite woman, tax collectors, the poor). Matthew 25:31-46 presents the final judgment as determined by how one treated the least, the hungry, the imprisoned, the strangers. In a sense, Solomon's court becomes a type of Christ's judgment seat, where ultimate justice is rendered to those the world has forgotten.
commentary.application: Modern covenant members, especially those in positions of authority or influence, can apply Solomon's example by ensuring that their justice, mercy, and access extend to those at the margins of society—those without advocates, without power, without influence. In family, church, or community contexts, this means creating spaces where the voiceless can bring their grievances and be genuinely heard. Specific application: If you hold a position of leadership (bishop, Relief Society president, father, employer, teacher), do the marginalized in your sphere feel they can come before you and be heard? Are you accessible to those without political connections or social status? Solomon's very first test as a king with granted wisdom was to hear the case of two women society had written off. The principle applies to modern leadership.

text_kjv: And the one woman said, O my lord, I and this woman dwell in one house; and I was delivered of a child with her in the house.

commentary.narrative:
The first woman begins her statement with the respectful interjection "O my lord" (bi adoni—please, my lord), acknowledging the king's authority and status. She establishes the crucial facts of the case: she and the other woman share a dwelling (bayit echad, "one house"), and at the time of her childbirth, the other woman was present in the same house with no third-party witnesses. The narrative is beginning to paint a picture of complete isolation from external observation—no midwife, no servant, no family member, no neutral witness was present to observe which child belonged to whom.

The phrase "I was delivered of a child" uses the verb yalad (to give birth, to bear). The first woman describes her delivery as a solitary event in the presence of only the second woman. The mutual confinement in the house—with the implication that both were in a state requiring confinement (the postpartum period of the ancient Near East)—means neither could easily leave or call for help. This establishes the evidentiary problem: there is no way to verify independently which woman gave birth to which child. In normal ancient Israelite law, this case would be nearly impossible to resolve. Multiple witnesses were required for testimony; a mother's word alone against another's would require additional evidence. But in this case, there are no witnesses to call, no documents to examine, no external facts to establish.

The woman's strategy is to lay out the facts clearly and completely, hoping that the king will believe her account over the other woman's. She is not making specific accusations yet but establishing the context: same house, simultaneous confinement, complete isolation. The legal problem is about to become more severe: verse 18 will reveal that one of the children died, and now both women claim the living child as their own. With no way to verify birth order, no medical examination possible, and no witnesses, how can justice be determined?

word_study.meaning: and she said; feminine singular past tense of amar, 'to say, to speak, to declare.'
word_study.significance: The verb is straightforward narrative speech, introducing the first woman's testimony. The feminine singular form establishes that this particular woman is speaking, distinguishing her from her companion.

word_study.meaning: please, my lord (literally, 'by me, my lord'); an interjection expressing respectful petition or address. The preposition bi can mean 'with me' or serve as an emphatic particle expressing appeal.
word_study.significance: The phrase acknowledges the king's superior status and the woman's humility in approaching him. She is not demanding but petitioning. The use of adoni ('my lord') rather than melekh ('king') conveys personal respect and deference. This is the language of a subject approaching a judge with a plea for justice.

word_study.meaning: dwelling, sitting, inhabiting; feminine plural from shevet, 'to sit, to dwell, to inhabit.' Used of permanent or semi-permanent residence.
word_study.significance: The verb yoshbot establishes that the two women were not temporary visitors to each other but long-term residents sharing a household. This eliminates the possibility that they were strangers or casual acquaintances.

word_study.meaning: I gave birth, I was delivered; first person singular past tense of yalad, 'to bear, to give birth.' Often used of the mother's action in bringing a child into the world.
word_study.significance: The verb yalad is precise and biological, used specifically for childbirth. The woman asserts her role as the biological mother of a child born in that house. The act of giving birth is framed as something she alone did, highlighting the isolation and the lack of witnesses to verify her claim.

word_study.meaning: in the house; the preposition be (in) + definite article + bayit (house). The definite article emphasizes the specific, shared dwelling.
word_study.significance: The repetition of 'the house' throughout verses 17-18 emphasizes the enclosed space where both women were confined together. The house becomes the entire world of their case—nothing outside it can corroborate their stories.

cross_references.connection: The law requires 'At the mouth of two witnesses, or three witnesses, shall he that is worthy of death be put to death.' In normal legal procedure, testimony requires witnesses. The case before Solomon violates this principle—no witnesses exist for either woman's claim.

Later, after Solomon renders his judgment, 'all Israel heard of the judgment which the king had judged; and they feared the king: for they saw that the wisdom of God was in him.' Solomon's wisdom will be proven by his ability to determine truth in a case where normal legal procedures cannot apply.

Proverbs (attributed to Solomon) teaches: 'A true witness delivereth souls: but a deceitful witness speaketh lies.' This case will reveal whose testimony is true and whose is deceitful, with custody of a child at stake.

Job asks: 'What then shall I do when God riseth up? and when he visiteth, what shall I answer him?' Both the woman and the judge must face a truth-knowing reality higher than human perception. Solomon must access wisdom beyond human forensics.

commentary.historical_context: In ancient Israel, as in most ancient Near Eastern societies, childbirth was typically a women's affair. The birthing mother, midwives if available, and perhaps female relatives or servants would be present, but men ordinarily were excluded. In this case, two women—apparently alone with no midwife—gave birth to children without witnesses. In normal circumstances, the extended family and community would know the parentage of children born into the household. The isolation described here is unusual, perhaps suggesting that these women were servants or concubines in the royal household (though the text does not state this), or that they lived on the social margins without extended family support. The legal problem is real: ancient forensic science had no tools to determine parentage through birth timing or physical characteristics. The judge had to rely on testimony, witnesses, and circumstantial evidence. Without these, Solomon must discern truth through means beyond normal law.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: In Alma 32, Alma teaches that faith involves believing testimony when you cannot see with your own eyes. Similarly, Solomon must determine which woman's testimony is true when neither woman can produce external proof. The Book of Mormon principle of faith extends to legal judgment—sometimes the truth must be discerned spiritually when evidence is insufficient materially.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 88:63 teaches that 'the light shineth in the darkness, and the darkness comprehendeth it not.' Solomon must illuminate darkness—the hidden truth of which child belongs to which mother—through divine wisdom. The principle appears throughout Doctrine and Covenants that God's Spirit provides knowledge that human senses cannot access.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: In the temple, covenants are made before the Lord, and witnesses (the officiators) observe and testify to the making of covenants. In Solomon's court, the absence of witnesses creates a unique problem that only divine wisdom can solve. The principle suggests that when human witnesses are absent or inadequate, God's justice transcends normal legal procedure.

commentary.christological_typology: The woman's appeal to the king as her only recourse prefigures humanity's appeal to Jesus as the ultimate judge and advocate. Like the woman without witnesses or legal standing, fallen humanity has no independent claim to justice and must rely on the mercy and wisdom of the judge. The woman's respectful address ("O my lord") mirrors the posture the righteous are called to adopt before Christ—acknowledging His authority and appealing to His justice and mercy.
commentary.application: Verse 17 teaches the importance of establishing facts clearly and completely when presenting a case—whether in a family dispute, business conflict, or church discipline. The woman does not make accusations yet; she establishes the context. Modern application suggests that before leveling charges or seeking judgment, one should lay out the facts as completely as possible, acknowledging limitations in one's own knowledge. In conflicts within families or communities, honesty about what you know and what you do not know creates space for wisdom to operate. The woman's respectful tone ("O my lord") also models humility when approaching someone with authority—she is not demanding but petitioning. Modern covenant members seeking counsel or judgment should adopt a similar posture: clear in presenting facts, humble in acknowledging limitations, respectful toward those positioned to render judgment.

text_kjv: And it came to pass the third day after that I was delivered, that this woman was delivered also: and we were together; there was no stranger with us in the house, save we two in the house.

commentary.narrative:
The first woman continues her testimony, adding the crucial temporal detail: on the third day after she gave birth, the other woman also gave birth. The proximity in time and the complete isolation from any outside observer is now established beyond doubt. The phrase "we were together" (anachnu yachdav) emphasizes their simultaneous presence in the house—they shared the space, the experience, the knowledge of both births, but they witnessed each other without external corroboration. The repetition of the isolation formula—"there was no stranger with us in the house, save we two in the house"—drives home the evidentiary problem with almost legal redundancy. The phrase zar ("stranger, outsider") means anyone other than the two of them. There is no third party who can corroborate either woman's claim.

The problem is now fully articulated: Both women gave birth within days of each other, both are confined in the same house, both know what happened but only one speaks truth, and no external evidence exists to determine which child belongs to which mother. In verse 19 (not included in this passage), one of the children will die, and both women will claim the living child as their own. This is a test of wisdom that exceeds the capacity of normal law. Solomon cannot call witnesses who do not exist. He cannot demand documentary evidence. He cannot order a medical examination that would be meaningless—both children look like infants. He cannot apply a tie-breaking formula in Israelite law because no such formula exists for this precise situation.

Yet the narrator has set up the case to demonstrate the wisdom God granted Solomon. The test is not Solomon's knowledge of the law (any judge could recite the legal codes) but his ability to perceive truth beneath contradictory testimonies. The woman's repetition of the isolation—emphasizing it twice with parallel phrasing—suggests either genuine credibility (she is thoroughly establishing the context) or legal anxiety (she is nervous and over-explaining). The reader cannot yet determine which. Solomon's wisdom will need to penetrate not just the facts but the character and motivations of the speakers themselves.

word_study.meaning: and it came to pass, and it was, and it happened; from the root h-y-h, 'to be, to exist, to occur.' A common narrative formula introducing a new development in a story.
word_study.significance: The formula vayehi marks the progression from the initial context (they live in the same house) to the temporal development (the specific timing of the births). It moves the narrative forward toward the central problem.

word_study.meaning: on the third day, on the third day after; bayom (on the day) + hashelishi (the third). The definite article and ordinal number specify a precise time reference.
word_study.significance: The third day is significant in biblical narrative, often marking a turning point or revelation (Genesis 22:4, Jonah 1:17, 1 Corinthians 15:4). Here it marks the point at which the second birth occurred, creating a narrow temporal window for two births in the same house.

word_study.meaning: together, united, at the same time; from the root ch-d-d, meaning 'to be one, to unite.' The adverb emphasizes simultaneity and proximity.
word_study.significance: The word yachdav conveys not just that the births happened close in time but that the two women shared the experience, lived through the same period together. They were not separated; they inhabited the same space during both births.

word_study.meaning: no stranger, no outsider, no one else; ein (not, no) + zar (stranger, outsider, foreigner). The term zar can mean a non-Israelite, a non-family member, or simply 'another person.'
word_study.significance: The word zar establishes the critical evidentiary vacuum. A zar would have been a third-party witness—the very thing that is absent. The Covenant Rendering notes that zar means 'anyone other than the two of them.' The legal problem is absolute: no tertium quid (third thing, external evidence) exists.

word_study.meaning: except for/save us two; zulati (except, save, except for) + shetayim (the two of us, feminine dual). The phrase emphasizes exclusivity—only these two.
word_study.significance: The repetition of the isolation in different grammatical form (ein zar... zulati shetayim—'no stranger... except us two') creates a legal parallelism that emphasizes the evidentiary void. The narrator is mimicking legal testimony's careful redundancy, as if the woman is explaining the problem to ensure the judge understands its severity.

cross_references.connection: The case continues with one child dying, both women claiming the living child, and Solomon's famous judgment to divide the child in two. Verse 18 establishes the legal problem to which verses 19-27 provide the miraculous solution.

Proverbs teaches: 'The heart of the prudent getteth knowledge; and the ear of the wise seeketh knowledge.' Solomon must listen carefully to the women's testimonies, discerning not just the words but the character and truth beneath them.

Proverbs (attributed to Solomon) teaches: 'Counsel in the heart of man is like deep water; but a man of understanding will draw it out.' Solomon must draw out the truth that lies beneath the surface testimony of both women—truth that is not obvious from the facts alone.

Jesus teaches: 'Judge not according to the appearance, but judge righteous judgment.' Like Jesus's teaching, Solomon's wisdom must penetrate beyond surface facts to discern the deeper truth of the women's hearts and claims.

The psalmist praises God: 'Thou knowest my downsitting and mine uprising, thou understandest my thought afar off.' Like God, Solomon must perceive what cannot be seen—the truth beneath contradictory testimonies.

commentary.historical_context: In ancient Israelite law, childbirth was typically attended by a midwife (mentioned in Genesis 35:17, Exodus 1:15-21). The presence of a midwife would have provided a witness to parentage. The absence of a midwife in this case is notable and unusual, suggesting that these women were either too poor to afford a midwife, too marginalized to have access to one, or (possibly) servants in the royal household living in separate quarters. The "house" (bayit) could refer to a small dwelling or a separate room within a larger compound. The legal problem created by the absence of witnesses reflects real gaps in ancient legal systems when cases fell outside normal social structures. A judge in such a case would need to rely on personal perception, character assessment, and (possibly) divination or oaths. Solomon will demonstrate that wisdom transcends these normal legal limitations.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: The Book of Mormon teaches repeatedly that hidden things are revealed to God and can be revealed through His servants. In Alma 18:32-33, King Lamoni is impressed by Ammon's apparent ability to perceive what would normally be hidden. Similarly, Solomon's wisdom will penetrate the hidden truth of which woman speaks truth and which lies. The principle is that God's servants, when granted divine wisdom, can perceive what the world cannot see.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 6:16 teaches: 'I am the light and the life of the world... and the light shineth in the darkness, and the darkness comprehendeth it not.' Solomon's wisdom is portrayed as a light that illuminates the darkness of competing testimonies and hidden truth. The principle appears throughout D&C that God's servants are given perception beyond natural means.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: In temple covenants, truth is established through divine knowledge rather than external witnesses. Similarly, Solomon's judgment will be rendered through divine wisdom perceiving truth that external witnesses cannot access. The principle suggests that the deepest truths are known and revealed only through connection to the divine, not through natural or legal procedures alone.

commentary.christological_typology: Both women claim the same child; both cannot be right. Similarly, in Matthew 21:25, Jesus asks the religious leaders whether John the Baptist's authority came from heaven or man. The answer determines everything about how one should respond to John and to Jesus. Truth cannot be compromised; two contradictory claims about parentage cannot both be true. Jesus, as the ultimate judge, has the ability (like Solomon) to determine truth that the world's normal procedures cannot establish. Jesus's authority as judge extends to determining the ultimate truth about identity, authority, and the human condition.
commentary.application: Verse 18 presents a model of careful testimony and factual establishment. The woman does not make accusations or attacks; she establishes facts clearly and completely, even with repetition to emphasize crucial points. In modern disputes within families, organizations, or communities, this model suggests that clear statement of facts (even if repeated for emphasis) is more effective than accusation or emotion. The woman is setting up a problem that only wisdom can solve. Similarly, when facing a difficult situation where normal procedures cannot resolve matters, the appropriate response is to lay out the facts clearly for those positioned to render judgment, then trust that genuine wisdom (whether divine or delegated) will penetrate to the truth. Application for parents: When children present conflicting accounts, resist the temptation to render judgment based on surface testimony. Like Solomon, discern the truth beneath the words by understanding character, motivation, and the deeper context. Application for leaders: When facing disputes with incomplete information, acknowledge the incompleteness honestly and seek the wisdom necessary to judge rightly.

text_kjv: And the king said, Divide the living child in two, and give half to the one, and half to the other.

commentary.narrative: Solomon's command appears, on its surface, to be an act of judicial horror—a pronouncement so brutal that it seems to violate every principle of justice and mercy. Yet this is precisely the point. Solomon, having received the gift of a "listening heart" in the previous chapter, now demonstrates the counterintuitive wisdom that undergirds true judgment. He does not attempt to determine which woman is the true mother through witness testimony or legal precedent. Instead, he engineers a situation that will force the truth to reveal itself. The command to divide the child is not a literal intention but a test—a stratagem that only genuine maternal love can survive intact. The TCR translation's emphasis on gizru ('cut!')—the imperative form—captures the sharp, unsettling immediacy of the decree. Solomon is not deliberating or explaining; he is commanding, with the full authority of the monarchy behind his words.
commentary.narrative_continued: This verse stands as the narrative hinge of the entire judgment scene. Everything before it is setup: the two harlots, the dispute, the king's initial position of ignorance. Everything after it is revelation: the true mother's involuntary response and the false mother's bitter acquiescence. The clinical language—lishnayim ('into two') and hachatsai...hachatsai ('half...half')—strips away sentiment and treats the child as an object to be divided. This dehumanization is deliberate. It is designed to shock the conscience of motherhood itself. By proposing to reduce the living child to a corpse split in two, Solomon creates a moral and emotional crucible. The one who birthed and nursed the child cannot endure this prospect. The one who merely covets him can.
commentary.narrative_continued_2: The genius of Solomon's approach lies in his understanding that justice sometimes cannot be adjudicated through traditional evidence or legal argument. When both parties claim the same child and both have a plausible narrative (the dead child scenario allows for confusion), the king must appeal to something deeper than testimony: the involuntary response of the human heart to threat and loss.
